stacks.title: The woman who made two powerful men fall
stacks.hook: Let's talk about the woman who made two of the most powerful men in the world fall for her. We're talking about Cleopatra.

cards.head: Let's talk about the woman who made two of the most powerful men in the world fall for her.
cards.body: We're talking about Cleopatra. She became the lover and political ally of both Julius Caesar and Mark Antony. But Cleopatra's ability to captivate powerful Romans was only one part of how she fought to preserve her throne.

cr.artwork: Cham - Charivari - V1d127-d.png
cr.file: Cham - Charivari - V1d127-d.png
cr.line: Cham - Charivari - V1d127-d.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SHE PROBABLY WASN'T THE MOST BEAUTIFUL WOMAN IN THE ROOM
cards.body: Plutarch, our main ancient source, writes that her beauty was not in itself incomparable, nor the sort to strike people who saw her. She was already queen of Egypt, so she did not need either man.

cr.artwork: Alma-tadema-antony-cleopatra.jpeg
cr.file: Alma-tadema-antony-cleopatra.jpeg
cr.line: Alma-tadema-antony-cleopatra.jpeg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SHE WASN'T ACTUALLY EGYPTIAN BY DYNASTY
cards.body: Cleopatra belonged to a Macedonian Greek dynasty descended from Ptolemy I, one of Alexander the Great's generals. Unlike many of her predecessors, ancient sources say Cleopatra actually learned Egyptian.

cr.artwork: Berlín Cleopatra 01.JPG
cr.file: Berlín Cleopatra 01.JPG
cr.line: Berlín Cleopatra 01.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SHE NEEDED TO GET TO JULIUS CAESAR
cards.body: Cleopatra was fighting her brother Ptolemy XIII for control of Egypt when Caesar arrived in Alexandria. The problem was getting into Caesar's quarters without her brother's forces stopping her.

cr.artwork: Head of Julius Caesar from Tusculum MAntTorino 2089 n01.jpg
cr.file: Head of Julius Caesar from Tusculum MAntTorino 2089 n01.jpg
cr.line: Head of Julius Caesar from Tusculum MAntTorino 2089 n01.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO SHE SMUGGLED HERSELF INSIDE
cards.body: According to Plutarch, Cleopatra had herself concealed inside a sack used for bedding and carried into Caesar's quarters. Later retellings transformed the sack into the famous story of Cleopatra dramatically rolling out of a carpet.

cr.artwork: Caesarion-Kleopatra Isis.jpg
cr.file: Caesarion-Kleopatra Isis.jpg
cr.line: Caesarion-Kleopatra Isis.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: IT WORKED
cards.body: Caesar backed Cleopatra in the struggle for Egypt, and she regained her throne. They also became lovers, and Cleopatra later gave birth to Caesarion, whom she claimed was Caesar's son.

cr.artwork: Ptolemy I British Museum.jpg
cr.file: Ptolemy I British Museum.jpg
cr.line: Ptolemy I British Museum.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN CAME MARK ANTONY
cards.body: Years after Caesar's assassination, Cleopatra formed another political and romantic partnership with Mark Antony. Together they had three children and eventually became the greatest threat to Caesar's heir, Octavian.

cr.artwork: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg
cr.file: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg
cr.line: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HER DEFEAT HELPED CREATE AN EMPEROR
cards.body: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra, and both died in 30 BCE. Egypt became Roman territory, while Octavian became Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

cr.artwork: Beeldhouwwerk Augustus van Prima Porta Caesar Augustus, Vatican (titel op object), RP-F-F01143-CK.jpg
cr.file: Beeldhouwwerk Augustus van Prima Porta Caesar Augustus, Vatican (titel op object), RP-F-F01143-CK.jpg
cr.line: Beeldhouwwerk Augustus van Prima Porta Caesar Augustus, Vatican (titel op object), RP-F-F01143-CK.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE BEAUTY MYTH PERSISTS
cards.body: Saying she was clever means Rome was outmanoeuvred. Saying she was beautiful means Rome was bewitched. Only one of those lets the losing side keep its dignity.

cr.file: Cleopatra and Caesar alternate.jpg
cr.line: Cleopatra and Caesar alternate.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Lincoln kept losing
stacks.hook: He lost elections, buried the woman he loved, and still saved the nation that never made anything easy for him.

cards.head: He lost elections, buried the woman he loved, and still saved the nation that never made anything easy for him.
cards.body: Abraham Lincoln's path to the presidency was filled with political defeats, poverty and personal loss. His rise looks far less inevitable when you see what happened before 1860.

cards.head: HE STARTED WITH ALMOST NOTHING
cards.body: Lincoln was born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky in 1809 and received little formal schooling. He largely educated himself and eventually became a lawyer.

cr.artwork: Mary Todd Lincoln 1846-1847 restored cropped.png
cr.file: Mary Todd Lincoln 1846-1847 restored cropped.png
cr.line: Mary Todd Lincoln 1846-1847 restored cropped.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS FIRST ELECTION WAS A LOSS
cards.body: At 23, Lincoln ran for the Illinois legislature and lost. He tried again two years later, won and eventually served four terms before becoming a U.S. congressman.

cr.artwork: Lincoln Cabin, Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site (7eae8bbd-d5ca-410a-b05d-4f92cd2cc2bf).jpg
cr.file: Lincoln Cabin, Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site (7eae8bbd-d5ca-410a-b05d-4f92cd2cc2bf).jpg
cr.line: Lincoln Cabin, Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site (7eae8bbd-d5ca-410a-b05d-4f92cd2cc2bf).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN ANN RUTLEDGE DIED
cards.body: As a young man, Lincoln was extremely close to Ann Rutledge, who died at just 22, probably from typhoid fever. Later accounts portrayed Lincoln as devastated, although historians still debate exactly how romantic their relationship was.

cards.head: HIS CAREER KEPT STALLING
cards.body: Lincoln failed in attempts to become a U.S. senator and lost the famous 1858 Senate race to Stephen Douglas. But their debates over slavery turned Lincoln from an Illinois politician into a national figure.

cr.artwork: Abraham Lincoln O-121 by Gardner, 1863.jpg
cr.file: Abraham Lincoln O-121 by Gardner, 1863.jpg
cr.line: Abraham Lincoln O-121 by Gardner, 1863.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN HE WON THE PRESIDENCY
cards.body: In 1860, Lincoln won the presidency despite receiving less than 40 percent of the popular vote and virtually no support in the slaveholding South. Almost immediately, Southern states began seceding.

cr.artwork: AL1860.jpg
cr.file: AL1860.jpg
cr.line: AL1860.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE MAN WHO KEPT LOSING HAD TO SAVE THE UNION
cards.body: Weeks after Lincoln took office, the Civil War began. The politician whose career had repeatedly seemed finished was suddenly responsible for holding the United States together.

cr.line: Log Cabin - Lincoln Birthplace NHS - Aug 2017.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE FAILURE LIST GETS SHARED
cards.body: The reassuring version of Lincoln, a man who lost constantly and then saved a country, is repeated so often that most people meet the losses before they meet the presidency.

stacks.title: Galatians 5: the fruit test
stacks.hook: If someone showed up at your front doorstep right now with a basket of fruit and asked you to let them in, and you look in that basket and the fruit is rotten. It is gross. Looks like it's been sitting in the sun for 10 days. What are you doing? Let's unpack Galatians chapter 5.

cards.head: If someone showed up at your front doorstep right now with a basket of fruit and asked you to let them in, and you look in that basket and the fruit is rotten.
cards.body: It is gross. Looks like it's been sitting in the sun for 10 days. What are you doing?

cr.artwork: Basket of Fruit-Caravaggio (c.1595).jpg
cr.file: Basket of Fruit-Caravaggio (c.1595).jpg
cr.line: Basket of Fruit-Caravaggio (c.1595).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: Let's unpack Galatians chapter 5.
cards.body: Paul uses fruit as a metaphor for something surprisingly practical: you can tell what is happening inside someone by looking at what their life produces.

cr.artwork: Frédéric Lix, Les Vendanges.jpg
cr.file: Frédéric Lix, Les Vendanges.jpg
cr.line: Frédéric Lix, Les Vendanges.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: PAUL SAYS THERE ARE TWO KINDS OF FRUIT
cards.body: Galatians 5 contrasts living according to the "flesh" with living according to the Spirit. By "flesh," Paul means human desires operating against God's will, not simply the physical body.

cr.artwork: Edgar Barclay (1842-1913) - The Grape Harvest - H5467 - Hospitalfield House.jpg
cr.file: Edgar Barclay (1842-1913) - The Grape Harvest - H5467 - Hospitalfield House.jpg
cr.line: Edgar Barclay (1842-1913) - The Grape Harvest - H5467 - Hospitalfield House.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THIS IS THE ROTTEN FRUIT
cards.body: Paul's list includes sexual immorality, jealousy, hatred, rage, selfish ambition, envy and drunkenness. His point is that destructive patterns reveal what is governing someone's life.
cards.cap: Unknown (possibly, school of Simon Bening or a follower of Horenbout working in England)

cr.line: British Library MS. Royal 1 E V - folio 5 - St. Paul Writing His Epistles with John Colet.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN COMES THE GOOD FRUIT
cards.body: Paul contrasts those behaviors with nine qualities known as the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

cr.artwork: Handbook of ornament; a grammar of art, industrial and architectural designing in all its branches, for practical as well as theoretical use (1900) (14597855857).jpg

cr.line: Handbook of ornament; a grammar of art, industrial and architectural designing in all its branches, for practical as well as theoretical use (1900) (14597855857).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: NOTICE HE CALLS IT "FRUIT," NOT "RULES"
cards.body: The metaphor matters because fruit grows naturally from what a plant is rooted in. Paul's argument is that a life guided by God's Spirit should gradually produce recognizable characteristics.

cr.artwork: Ann Arbor, University of Michigan P.Mich.inv. 6238 (Papyrus 46) fol. 158r Eph 6, 20–Gal 1, 8.jpg
cr.file: Ann Arbor, University of Michigan P.Mich.inv. 6238 (Papyrus 46) fol. 158r Eph 6, 20–Gal 1, 8.jpg
cr.line: Ann Arbor, University of Michigan P.Mich.inv. 6238 (Papyrus 46) fol. 158r Eph 6, 20–Gal 1, 8.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO LOOK AT WHAT SOMEONE PRODUCES
cards.body: Someone can tell you they're loving, spiritual or good, but Paul gives Christians a different test. Look at the actual fruit: are their actions producing love and peace, or jealousy, anger and division?

cr.artwork: Lotz Allegory of Grape Harvest.jpg
cr.file: Lotz Allegory of Grape Harvest.jpg
cr.line: Lotz Allegory of Grape Harvest.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND THE SAME TEST APPLIES TO YOU
cards.body: Galatians 5 isn't primarily a tool for judging everyone around you. Paul's challenge is to examine what your own life is consistently producing, because eventually the fruit reveals the tree.

cards.head: WHY THIS TEST OUTLASTED THE LETTER
cards.body: It gives you something to look at instead of something to believe. A rule you can apply to your own week survives longer than a doctrine you have to accept.

stacks.title: Mary Magdalene wasn't a prostitute
stacks.hook: They called her a prostitute, but she was actually a prophet. Here's what they don't teach about Mary Magdalene.

cards.head: They called her a prostitute, but she was actually a prophet.
cards.body: Here's what they don't teach about Mary Magdalene. The Bible never calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute. Instead, she appears as one of Jesus's most devoted followers and becomes one of the central witnesses to his resurrection.
cards.cap: Georges de La Tour Magdalen of Night Light WGA12337

cr.artwork: Georges de La Tour - Magdalen of Night Light - WGA12337.jpg
cr.file: Georges de La Tour - Magdalen of Night Light - WGA12337.jpg
cr.line: Georges de La Tour - Magdalen of Night Light - WGA12337.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE PROSTITUTE STORY CAME CENTURIES LATER
cards.body: In 591 CE, Pope Gregory I famously associated Mary Magdalene with an unnamed "sinful woman" in the Gospel of Luke. That interpretation shaped Western Christianity for centuries, even though the biblical text never identifies the women as the same person.

cr.artwork: Noli-me-tangere-titien.jpg
cr.file: Noli-me-tangere-titien.jpg
cr.line: Noli-me-tangere-titien.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: MARY ACTUALLY TRAVELED WITH JESUS
cards.body: Luke says Jesus had healed Mary of "seven demons," after which she traveled with him and the disciples. She was also among a group of women who financially supported Jesus's ministry.

cr.artwork: Caravaggio, Michelangelo Merisi da - Martha and Mary Magdalene - c. 1598.jpg
cr.file: Caravaggio, Michelangelo Merisi da - Martha and Mary Magdalene - c. 1598.jpg
cr.line: Caravaggio, Michelangelo Merisi da - Martha and Mary Magdalene - c. 1598.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SHE DIDN'T ABANDON HIM AT THE CROSS
cards.body: The Gospels explicitly place Mary Magdalene at Jesus's crucifixion and burial. Then she returns to his tomb after his death and discovers it empty.

cr.artwork: Carracci, Annibale -- The Penitent Magdalen in a Landscape - c. 1598.jpg
cr.file: Carracci, Annibale -- The Penitent Magdalen in a Landscape - c. 1598.jpg
cr.line: Carracci, Annibale -- The Penitent Magdalen in a Landscape - c. 1598.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: JESUS APPEARED TO HER FIRST
cards.body: In the Gospel of John, Mary is the first person to encounter the resurrected Jesus. Jesus then tells her to go announce what happened to his other disciples.

cr.artwork: Gaspar de Crayer – The Crucifixion with Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Francis.jpg
cr.file: Gaspar de Crayer – The Crucifixion with Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Francis.jpg
cr.line: Gaspar de Crayer – The Crucifixion with Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Francis.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THERE'S EVEN A GOSPEL OF MARY
cards.body: A noncanonical early Christian text called the Gospel of Mary portrays Mary receiving a revelation from Jesus and teaching the other disciples. Peter challenges her authority, while another disciple, Levi, defends her.

cr.artwork: Gospel of Mary.jpg
cr.file: Gospel of Mary.jpg
cr.line: Gospel of Mary.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO WAS MARY ACTUALLY A PROPHET?
cards.body: Calling her a "prophet" is an interpretation rather than a title the canonical Gospels explicitly give her. But the biblical Mary is far closer to a disciple, witness and messenger of Jesus than the prostitute she was later portrayed as.

cr.artwork: Ambrosius Benson - Mary Magdalene - WGA01889.jpg
cr.file: Ambrosius Benson - Mary Magdalene - WGA01889.jpg
cr.line: Ambrosius Benson - Mary Magdalene - WGA01889.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE CORRECTION CAME TOO LATE
cards.body: The prostitute reading entered the church in 591 and was formally undone in 1969. Centuries of paintings, sermons and plays had already fixed her, and art does not issue retractions.

cr.artwork: Andrea di Bartolo - The Resurrection - Walters 37741.jpg
cr.file: Andrea di Bartolo - The Resurrection - Walters 37741.jpg
cr.line: Andrea di Bartolo - The Resurrection - Walters 37741.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Georges de La Tour, The Penitent Magdalen, c. 1640, The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Why did they actually kill Jesus?
stacks.hook: Why did they actually kill Jesus?

cards.head: Why did they actually kill Jesus?
cards.body: Christians understand Jesus's death theologically as a sacrifice for humanity's sins. But historically, crucifixion was a Roman execution, so to understand why Jesus died, you have to understand why Roman authorities considered him dangerous.

cr.artwork: Christ Cleansing the Temple by El Greco - Q63117265.jpg
cr.file: Christ Cleansing the Temple by El Greco - Q63117265.jpg
cr.line: Christ Cleansing the Temple by El Greco - Q63117265.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: JESUS WASN'T EXECUTED FOR SIMPLY PREACHING LOVE
cards.body: Jesus preached about the "Kingdom of God," attracted large crowds and entered Jerusalem during Passover, when the city was packed with pilgrims. Roman authorities were particularly sensitive to potential unrest during major Jewish festivals.

cr.artwork: Antonio Ciseri - Ecce Homo.jpg
cr.file: Antonio Ciseri - Ecce Homo.jpg
cr.line: Antonio Ciseri - Ecce Homo.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN JESUS ENTERED THE TEMPLE
cards.body: The Gospels describe Jesus overturning tables and disrupting commerce in the Jerusalem Temple. Whatever its exact scale, this was a provocative public act at the religious and political center of Judea.

cr.artwork: Brugghen Pilate washing his hands 01.jpg
cr.file: Brugghen Pilate washing his hands 01.jpg
cr.line: Brugghen Pilate washing his hands 01.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOME JEWISH AUTHORITIES WANTED HIM STOPPED
cards.body: The Gospels portray leading Jewish authorities as viewing Jesus as dangerous or blasphemous and handing him over to the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. Historians caution against turning this into collective blame of Jews; the final power to impose crucifixion belonged to Rome.

cr.artwork: Crucifixion Grunewald.jpg
cr.file: Crucifixion Grunewald.jpg
cr.line: Crucifixion Grunewald.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN COMES THE POLITICAL ACCUSATION
cards.body: Jesus was accused before Pilate of presenting himself as the "King of the Jews." In a province ruled by Rome, claiming kingship could be interpreted as a challenge to Caesar's authority.

cr.artwork: Jesus King of the Jews at the Cathedral.jpg
cr.file: Jesus King of the Jews at the Cathedral.jpg
cr.line: Jesus King of the Jews at the Cathedral.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: LOOK AT WHAT ROME PUT ABOVE HIS HEAD
cards.body: The Gospels say a sign was placed over Jesus during his crucifixion identifying him as "King of the Jews." Whatever theological meanings Christians later attached to his death, the charge displayed at his execution was unmistakably political.

cr.artwork: Jerusalem Modell BW 2.JPG
cr.file: Jerusalem Modell BW 2.JPG
cr.line: Jerusalem Modell BW 2.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THAT'S WHY CRUCIFIXION MATTERS
cards.body: Rome commonly used crucifixion as a brutal public punishment, particularly against slaves, rebels and people perceived as threats to Roman order. Historically, Jesus was executed by the Roman state under Pontius Pilate; Christianity then built its central theological claim around what his death and resurrection meant.

cr.artwork: ElGrecoCleansing.jpg
cr.file: ElGrecoCleansing.jpg
cr.line: ElGrecoCleansing.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE QUESTION KEEPS REOPENING
cards.body: The theological answer and the historical answer are different questions, and people keep hearing one when the other was asked. That mismatch is why this argument never closes.

cr.artwork: Caesarea maritima BW 5.JPG
cr.file: Caesarea maritima BW 5.JPG
cr.line: Caesarea maritima BW 5.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.artwork: El Greco, Christ Driving the Money Changers from the Temple, c. 1600
cr.line: El Greco, Christ Driving the Money Changers from the Temple, c. 1600. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.artwork: Mihaly Munkacsy, Christ before Pilate, 1881

stacks.title: NASA and the darkness at the crucifixion
stacks.hook: NASA has done research connected to the crucifixion of Christ.

cards.head: NASA has done research connected to the crucifixion of Christ.
cards.body: But not because NASA was trying to prove Christianity. NASA-associated astronomical calculations have been used in discussions of an unusual darkness described in biblical accounts of Jesus's crucifixion.
cards.cap: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - USRA/Ernie Wright

cr.artwork: March 3, 2026 Total Lunar Eclipse- Telescopic View (SVS5605 - lain preview).jpg
cr.file: March 3, 2026 Total Lunar Eclipse- Telescopic View (SVS5605 - lain preview).jpg
cr.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio - USRA/Ernie Wright
cr.line: March 3, 2026 Total Lunar Eclipse- Telescopic View (SVS5605 - lain preview).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE GOSPELS DESCRIBE THE SKY GOING DARK
cards.body: The Synoptic Gospels say darkness covered the land for roughly three hours while Jesus was on the cross. That has led people for centuries to ask whether an astronomical event could explain the story.

cr.artwork: Anthony van Dyck - Christ on the Cross - WGA07431.jpg
cr.file: Anthony van Dyck - Christ on the Cross - WGA07431.jpg
cr.line: Anthony van Dyck - Christ on the Cross - WGA07431.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: IT COULDN'T HAVE BEEN A SOLAR ECLIPSE
cards.body: Passover occurs around a full moon, while solar eclipses require a new moon. A normal solar eclipse also cannot produce three hours of total darkness in one location.

cr.artwork: Christ Crucified Between the Two Thieves (The Three Crosses) MET DP815616.jpg
cr.file: Christ Crucified Between the Two Thieves (The Three Crosses) MET DP815616.jpg
cr.line: Christ Crucified Between the Two Thieves (The Three Crosses) MET DP815616.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT THERE WAS A LUNAR ECLIPSE
cards.body: Astronomical calculations show that a partial lunar eclipse occurred on April 3, 33 CE, one proposed date for Jesus's crucifixion. The eclipse would have been visible from Jerusalem around moonrise.

cr.artwork: Blood moon over Brastad old cemetery.jpg
cr.file: Blood moon over Brastad old cemetery.jpg
cr.line: Blood moon over Brastad old cemetery.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE MOON MAY HAVE APPEARED RED
cards.body: During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow can cause the moon to appear reddish. Some researchers have connected this with Acts describing the moon turning "to blood," although that passage itself quotes the prophet Joel and does not prove the eclipse theory.

cr.artwork: Crucifixion-1896.jpg
cr.file: Crucifixion-1896.jpg
cr.line: Crucifixion-1896.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: DOES THIS PROVE THE CRUCIFIXION?
cards.body: No. Astronomical calculations can tell us what the sky was doing on a particular ancient date, but they cannot establish that a biblical event occurred or determine its supernatural meaning.

cr.artwork: Eggs- facts and fancies about them (1890) (14770995444).jpg
cr.file: Eggs- facts and fancies about them (1890) (14770995444).jpg
cr.line: Eggs- facts and fancies about them (1890) (14770995444).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT IT GIVES HISTORIANS ANOTHER CLUE
cards.body: Researchers have used Passover dates, Roman history and astronomical events to investigate possible dates for Jesus's death. April 3, 33 CE remains one proposed date, but scholars have not reached a universal consensus.

cr.artwork: Morton solar eclipse 1869-Aug-07.jpg
cr.file: Morton solar eclipse 1869-Aug-07.jpg
cr.line: Morton solar eclipse 1869-Aug-07.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY PEOPLE WANT THE SKY TO CONFIRM IT
cards.body: An eclipse would move the story out of belief and into the record. The appeal is not the astronomy, it is the idea that something checkable might be hiding inside a text you cannot check.

cr.artwork: Crucifixion by G.Margkazinis (17th c.).jpg
cr.file: Crucifixion by G.Margkazinis (17th c.).jpg
cr.line: Crucifixion by G.Margkazinis (17th c.).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.credit: NASA Glenn Research Center / NASA/Jordan Cochran
cr.line: NASA photograph of a total lunar eclipse 'blood moon'. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: The Gnostics
stacks.hook: Why did some early Christians believe the Christian God was evil?

cards.head: Why did some early Christians believe the Christian God was evil?
cards.body: They didn't exactly believe the highest God was evil. Some movements now grouped under "Gnosticism" believed something much stranger: the being who created our physical world wasn't the highest God at all.

cr.artwork: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg
cr.file: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg
cr.line: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEY BELIEVED IN A HIGHER GOD
cards.body: Many Gnostic systems described a perfect, unknowable God existing beyond the material universe. The physical world, with all its suffering and imperfection, seemed incompatible with such a perfect being.

cr.artwork: Cranach - Friedländer and Rosenberg, 202.jpg
cr.file: Cranach - Friedländer and Rosenberg, 202.jpg
cr.line: Cranach - Friedländer and Rosenberg, 202.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO WHO CREATED OUR WORLD?
cards.body: Some Gnostics said the material universe was created by an inferior being commonly called the Demiurge. Depending on the tradition, the Demiurge could be ignorant, arrogant or actively malevolent.

cr.artwork: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach (I).jpg
cr.file: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach (I).jpg
cr.line: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach (I).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOME IDENTIFIED HIM WITH THE GOD OF THE OLD TESTAMENT
cards.body: Certain Gnostic Christians interpreted the creator described in the Hebrew Bible as this lesser being.

cr.artwork: The Fall of Man by Lukas Cranach.jpg
cr.file: The Fall of Man by Lukas Cranach.jpg
cr.line: The Fall of Man by Lukas Cranach.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: When he declares himself the only God, they interpreted it not as proof of his supremacy, but as evidence that he didn't know the higher God existed.

cr.artwork: Henri Rousseau, ca.1905-07, Eve and the Serpent, oil on canvas, 61 x 46 cm, Kunsthalle Hamburg, Germany.jpg
cr.file: Henri Rousseau, ca.1905-07, Eve and the Serpent, oil on canvas, 61 x 46 cm, Kunsthalle Hamburg, Germany.jpg
cr.line: Henri Rousseau, ca.1905-07, Eve and the Serpent, oil on canvas, 61 x 46 cm, Kunsthalle Hamburg, Germany.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THAT COMPLETELY CHANGES THE GARDEN OF EDEN
cards.body: In some Gnostic traditions, the command preventing Adam and Eve from gaining knowledge becomes suspicious. Some even reinterpret the serpent as helping humanity obtain knowledge that the creator wanted to keep from them.

cr.artwork: Hans Baldung Grien - Eve, Serpent and Death.JPG
cr.file: Hans Baldung Grien - Eve, Serpent and Death.JPG
cr.line: Hans Baldung Grien - Eve, Serpent and Death.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN JESUS ARRIVES
cards.body: In these systems, Jesus comes from the higher divine realm to reveal the truth about humanity's origins. Salvation therefore comes through gnosis, or spiritual knowledge, that awakens the divine spark trapped within humans.

cr.artwork: Coptic Liturgical Codex MET DP100664.jpg
cr.file: Coptic Liturgical Codex MET DP100664.jpg
cr.line: Coptic Liturgical Codex MET DP100664.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THIS VERSION OF CHRISTIANITY LOST
cards.body: Christians who believed the creator was the one true God ultimately became the dominant tradition and condemned Gnostic teachings as heresy. But texts discovered near Nag Hammadi in 1945 revealed just how radically different some ancient interpretations of Christianity had been.

cr.artwork: Lucas Cranach d. Ä. 035.jpg
cr.file: Lucas Cranach d. Ä. 035.jpg
cr.line: Lucas Cranach d. Ä. 035.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE LOSING SIDE FASCINATES US
cards.body: For centuries the Gnostics were known only through the writings of people refuting them. Then a jar turned up in 1945 and they finally spoke in their own voice. Almost nothing else in ancient history got that.

cr.artwork: William Blake Eve Tempted by the Serpent.jpg
cr.file: William Blake Eve Tempted by the Serpent.jpg
cr.line: William Blake Eve Tempted by the Serpent.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.credit: Unknown author Unknown author (attributed to Thomas)
cr.line: Page 36 of Nag Hammadi Codex II, containing the Gospel of Thomas, 4th century, Coptic Museum, Cairo. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Cleopatra's four children
stacks.hook: Cleopatra had four children. One was executed, three were taken to Rome, and then they basically disappeared from history.

cards.head: Cleopatra had four children.
cards.body: One was executed, three were taken to Rome, and then they basically disappeared from history. Cleopatra had one son with Julius Caesar and three children with Mark Antony. What happened to them after their parents died is one of the strangest epilogues to Cleopatra's story.

cr.artwork: Caesarion-Kleopatra Isis.jpg
cr.file: Caesarion-Kleopatra Isis.jpg
cr.line: Caesarion-Kleopatra Isis.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HER FIRST SON WAS CAESAR'S
cards.body: In 47 BCE, Cleopatra gave birth to Ptolemy XV, better known as Caesarion, meaning "Little Caesar." Cleopatra presented him as Julius Caesar's son, although Caesar never formally made him his heir.

cr.artwork: Cleopatra Selene Obverse.jpg
cr.file: Cleopatra Selene Obverse.jpg
cr.line: Cleopatra Selene Obverse.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN SHE HAD THREE CHILDREN WITH MARK ANTONY
cards.body: Cleopatra and Antony had twins, Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene II, followed by another son, Ptolemy Philadelphus. Their names reflected their parents' enormous ambitions for a new dynasty spanning the eastern Mediterranean.

cr.artwork: Bust of Juba II.jpg
cr.file: Bust of Juba II.jpg
cr.line: Bust of Juba II.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN THEIR PARENTS LOST EVERYTHING
cards.body: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra, invaded Egypt and captured Alexandria in 30 BCE. Antony and Cleopatra both died, leaving their children at the mercy of the man who had destroyed their empire.

cr.artwork: Beeldhouwwerk Augustus van Prima Porta Caesar Augustus, Vatican (titel op object), RP-F-F01143-CK.jpg
cr.file: Beeldhouwwerk Augustus van Prima Porta Caesar Augustus, Vatican (titel op object), RP-F-F01143-CK.jpg
cr.line: Beeldhouwwerk Augustus van Prima Porta Caesar Augustus, Vatican (titel op object), RP-F-F01143-CK.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: OCTAVIAN HAD CAESARION KILLED
cards.body: Caesarion potentially had the most dangerous claim of all because Cleopatra presented him as Caesar's biological son. Octavian had the teenage Caesarion executed, reportedly after being advised that "too many Caesars is not good."

cr.artwork: Roman Forum (Forum Romanum) Arch of Titus (48416928981).jpg
cr.file: Roman Forum (Forum Romanum) Arch of Titus (48416928981).jpg
cr.line: Roman Forum (Forum Romanum) Arch of Titus (48416928981).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN HE PARADED THE OTHER CHILDREN THROUGH ROME
cards.body: Antony and Cleopatra's three surviving children were taken to Rome and displayed in Octavian's triumph. Then, bizarrely, they were placed in the household of Octavia, Octavian's sister and Mark Antony's former wife.

cr.artwork: Ptolemaic Prince LACMA M.80.199.28.jpg
cr.file: Ptolemaic Prince LACMA M.80.199.28.jpg
cr.line: Ptolemaic Prince LACMA M.80.199.28.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: ONLY ONE CHILD'S FATE IS CLEAR
cards.body: Cleopatra Selene survived, married King Juba II and became queen of Mauretania in North Africa, where she continued elements of her mother's Ptolemaic legacy. What ultimately happened to her two brothers is uncertain because they disappear from the surviving historical record.

cr.artwork: Cleopatra and Caesarion with the gods.png
cr.file: Cleopatra and Caesarion with the gods.png
cr.line: Cleopatra and Caesarion with the gods.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE CHILDREN HAUNT THE STORY
cards.body: Three of them walk into a Roman triumph and then out of the record entirely. History rarely loses people that visible, and the silence is louder than an ending would be.

cr.artwork: Berlín Cleopatra 01.JPG
cr.file: Berlín Cleopatra 01.JPG
cr.line: Berlín Cleopatra 01.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.cap: Relief of Cleopatra VII and her son Caesarion on the Temple of Hathor at Dendera

cr.artwork: Relief of Cleopatra VII and her son Caesarion on the Temple of Hathor at Dendera
cr.line: Relief of Cleopatra VII and her son Caesarion on the Temple of Hathor at Dendera. Photo: Olaf Tausch, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Lincoln wasn't the only target
stacks.hook: Lincoln wasn't supposed to be the only person assassinated that night.

cards.head: Lincoln wasn't supposed to be the only person assassinated that night.
cards.body: John Wilkes Booth's plan wasn't simply to kill Abraham Lincoln. On April 14, 1865, conspirators were supposed to simultaneously attack the president, vice president and secretary of state.

cr.artwork: Abraham Lincoln - Sixteenth President of the United States - Assassinated April 14th, 1865 - Currier & Ives.jpg
cr.file: Abraham Lincoln - Sixteenth President of the United States - Assassinated April 14th, 1865 - Currier & Ives.jpg
cr.line: Abraham Lincoln - Sixteenth President of the United States - Assassinated April 14th, 1865 - Currier & Ives.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BOOTH WANTED TO DESTROY THE GOVERNMENT
cards.body: The Civil War was effectively ending, and Booth was a Confederate sympathizer furious about the South's defeat. He hoped that killing several of America's leaders at once could throw the federal government into chaos.

cr.artwork: Lewis Payne.jpg
cr.file: Lewis Payne.jpg
cr.line: Lewis Payne.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BOOTH TOOK LINCOLN
cards.body: Booth assigned himself the president. That night, he entered Lincoln's box at Ford's Theatre and shot him in the back of the head before escaping on horseback.

cr.artwork: (Agen) Portrait du jeune Bridger Seward à la batte de cricket - Ozias Humphrey - Musée des Beaux-Arts d'Agen Joconde00870006540.jpg
cr.file: (Agen) Portrait du jeune Bridger Seward à la batte de cricket - Ozias Humphrey - Musée des Beaux-Arts d'Agen Joconde00870006540.jpg
cr.line: (Agen) Portrait du jeune Bridger Seward à la batte de cricket - Ozias Humphrey - Musée des Beaux-Arts d'Agen Joconde00870006540.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: ANOTHER MAN WENT AFTER THE SECRETARY OF STATE
cards.body: Lewis Powell was assigned to kill Secretary of State William Seward, who was recovering at home from a carriage accident. Powell forced his way inside and repeatedly stabbed Seward in his bed.

cr.artwork: -Presidential Campaign Medal with Portraits of Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson- MET DP269329.jpg
cr.file: -Presidential Campaign Medal with Portraits of Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson- MET DP269329.jpg
cr.line: -Presidential Campaign Medal with Portraits of Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson- MET DP269329.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOMEHOW, SEWARD SURVIVED
cards.body: Seward suffered horrific injuries, and several other people in the house were wounded. But a metal splint around Seward's injured jaw may have helped protect him from a fatal knife wound.

cr.artwork: Alexander Gardner - Execution of the Lincoln Assassination Conspirators. The Scaffold. - Google Art Project.jpg
cr.file: Alexander Gardner - Execution of the Lincoln Assassination Conspirators. The Scaffold. - Google Art Project.jpg
cr.line: Alexander Gardner - Execution of the Lincoln Assassination Conspirators. The Scaffold. - Google Art Project.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE VICE PRESIDENT'S ASSASSIN LOST HIS NERVE
cards.body: George Atzerodt was supposed to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson at his hotel. Instead, Atzerodt became frightened, never attempted the assassination and eventually fled.

cr.artwork: John-Wilkes-Booth--portrait.jpg
cr.file: John-Wilkes-Booth--portrait.jpg
cr.line: John-Wilkes-Booth--portrait.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: ONLY ONE OF THE THREE TARGETS DIED
cards.body: Lincoln died the following morning, but Johnson and Seward survived. Booth's attempt to decapitate the U.S. government failed, and after a massive 12-day manhunt, Booth himself was tracked to a Virginia farm and shot.

cr.artwork: The Assassination of President Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, Washington D.C., April 14th, 1865 MET DP831798.jpg
cr.file: The Assassination of President Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, Washington D.C., April 14th, 1865 MET DP831798.jpg
cr.line: The Assassination of President Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, Washington D.C., April 14th, 1865 MET DP831798.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE FULL PLOT IS FORGOTTEN
cards.body: One target died and the story simplified around him. A plan that mostly failed is harder to tell than a single shot, so the other two attacks dropped out of the telling.

cr.artwork: Lewis Powell in 1865 (3x4 cropped).jpg
cr.file: Lewis Powell in 1865 (3x4 cropped).jpg
cr.line: Lewis Powell in 1865 (3x4 cropped).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.artwork: Alexander Gardner, execution of the Lincoln conspirators, 7 July 1865
cr.line: Alexander Gardner, execution of the Lincoln conspirators, 7 July 1865. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Why did Jesus need to be betrayed?
stacks.hook: Judas betrayed Jesus for 30 pieces of silver. But why did Jesus need to be betrayed in the first place?

cards.head: Judas betrayed Jesus for 30 pieces of silver.
cards.body: But why did Jesus need to be betrayed in the first place? Jesus wasn't exactly hiding. He had preached publicly, entered Jerusalem in front of crowds and taught at the Temple, so Judas's role raises an obvious question.

cr.artwork: Giotto-KissofJudas.jpg
cr.file: Giotto-KissofJudas.jpg
cr.line: Giotto-KissofJudas.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE AUTHORITIES WANTED JESUS ARRESTED QUIETLY
cards.body: The Gospels describe religious authorities wanting to arrest Jesus while avoiding a public disturbance. Jerusalem was crowded for Passover, and Jesus had followers around him.

cr.artwork: Harmensz van Rijn Rembrandt (Bol, Ferdinad)(Jouderville, I.) (1606-1669) - Judas bringt die Silberlinge zurück - 1045 - Führermuseum.jpg
cr.file: Harmensz van Rijn Rembrandt (Bol, Ferdinad)(Jouderville, I.) (1606-1669) - Judas bringt die Silberlinge zurück - 1045 - Führermuseum.jpg
cr.line: Harmensz van Rijn Rembrandt (Bol, Ferdinad)(Jouderville, I.) (1606-1669) - Judas bringt die Silberlinge zurück - 1045 - Führermuseum.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: JUDAS COULD TELL THEM WHERE JESUS WOULD BE
cards.body: Judas was one of the Twelve and knew Jesus's movements. According to the Gospels, he agreed to lead an armed group to Jesus at night, away from the crowds.

cr.artwork: 'Agony in the Garden' by Ludovico Carracci .jpg
cr.file: 'Agony in the Garden' by Ludovico Carracci .jpg
cr.line: 'Agony in the Garden' by Ludovico Carracci .jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THAT'S WHERE THE KISS COMES FROM
cards.body: Judas arranged a signal identifying exactly whom they should arrest: the man he kissed. He approached Jesus in Gethsemane, greeted him and kissed him.

cr.artwork: 298 MS 65 F147 V.jpg
cr.file: 298 MS 65 F147 V.jpg
cr.line: 298 MS 65 F147 V.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE GOSPELS SAY MONEY WAS INVOLVED
cards.body: Matthew says the chief priests paid Judas 30 pieces of silver. But the Gospels give different emphases for his motivation, including money and Satanic influence, and historians cannot establish Judas's private motives.

cr.artwork: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) - The Last Supper (1495-1498).jpg
cr.file: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) - The Last Supper (1495-1498).jpg
cr.line: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) - The Last Supper (1495-1498).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN JUDAS REGRETTED IT
cards.body: According to Matthew, Judas tried to return the money after Jesus was condemned. He declared that he had betrayed innocent blood, threw the silver into the Temple and hanged himself.

cr.artwork: Bernhard Strigel - Christ Before the High Priest - Walters 37673.jpg
cr.file: Bernhard Strigel - Christ Before the High Priest - Walters 37673.jpg
cr.line: Bernhard Strigel - Christ Before the High Priest - Walters 37673.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT EVEN HIS DEATH HAS TWO VERSIONS
cards.body: Acts gives a different account, saying Judas acquired a field and died after falling and his body burst open. The disagreement between Matthew and Acts is one reason Judas remains one of the New Testament's most mysterious figures.

cr.artwork: Aceldama.png
cr.file: Aceldama.png
cr.line: Aceldama.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY JUDAS BECAME A COMMON NOUN
cards.body: His name is now the word for what he did. That is a rare fate for a historical figure, and it means the story is retold every time the word is used.

cr.artwork: Giotto - Scrovegni - -31- - Kiss of Judas.jpg
cr.file: Giotto - Scrovegni - -31- - Kiss of Judas.jpg
cr.line: Giotto - Scrovegni - -31- - Kiss of Judas.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Giotto, The Kiss of Judas, c. 1305, Scrovegni Chapel, Padua. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Giotto, Judas Receiving Payment for his Betrayal, Scrovegni Chapel, c. 1305. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Who decided which books got into the Bible?
stacks.hook: Who actually decided which books got into the Bible?

cards.head: Who actually decided which books got into the Bible?
cards.body: There wasn't one meeting where a group of people suddenly chose the Bible. The collection developed over centuries as early Christians debated which writings genuinely carried apostolic authority.

cr.artwork: Codex Sinaiticus Matthew 1,1-2,5.JPG
cr.file: Codex Sinaiticus Matthew 1,1-2,5.JPG
cr.line: Codex Sinaiticus Matthew 1,1-2,5.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EARLY CHRISTIANS HAD A LOT OF TEXTS
cards.body: Christian communities circulated the four familiar Gospels and Paul's letters, but also texts like the Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Peter, Shepherd of Hermas and Apocalypse of Peter. Different churches did not initially possess identical collections.

cr.artwork: Muratorian Fragment.jpg
cr.file: Muratorian Fragment.jpg
cr.line: Muratorian Fragment.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOME BOOKS BECAME ACCEPTED VERY EARLY
cards.body: By the late second century, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John were being treated by influential Christians as a four-Gospel collection. Paul's letters were also circulating together relatively early.

cr.artwork: Agios Germanos St Athanasius Church Chirist Icon 1816.JPG
cr.file: Agios Germanos St Athanasius Church Chirist Icon 1816.JPG
cr.line: Agios Germanos St Athanasius Church Chirist Icon 1816.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: OTHER BOOKS WERE DEBATED FOR CENTURIES
cards.body: Christians disagreed about texts including Revelation, Hebrews, James, 2 Peter and others. Meanwhile, some writings that were popular among Christians ultimately weren't included.

cr.artwork: First Council of Nicaea Michael Damaskinos.png
cr.file: First Council of Nicaea Michael Damaskinos.png
cr.line: First Council of Nicaea Michael Damaskinos.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: NO, CONSTANTINE DIDN'T CHOOSE THE BIBLE
cards.body: A popular story says Emperor Constantine or the Council of Nicaea decided which books belonged in Scripture in 325 CE. The surviving records of Nicaea show that its central controversy concerned the nature of Christ, not selecting the biblical canon.

cr.artwork: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg
cr.file: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg
cr.line: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE 27-BOOK LIST APPEARS IN 367 CE
cards.body: Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria wrote an Easter letter listing the same 27 New Testament books used by most Christians today. Other regional councils and church authorities later affirmed similar lists.

cr.artwork: Bifolio from Paul's Letter to the Romans, the end of Paul's Letter to the Philippians and the beginning of Paul's Letter to the Colossians.jpg
cr.file: Bifolio from Paul's Letter to the Romans, the end of Paul's Letter to the Philippians and the beginning of Paul's Letter to the Colossians.jpg
cr.line: Bifolio from Paul's Letter to the Romans, the end of Paul's Letter to the Philippians and the beginning of Paul's Letter to the Colossians.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO THE BIBLE EMERGED THROUGH A LONG PROCESS
cards.body: The New Testament wasn't secretly assembled overnight and alternative gospels weren't all removed at one dramatic council. It emerged through centuries of use, argument and decisions about which writings Christians considered authoritative.

cr.artwork: Fragments of the Colossus of Constantine, courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome.jpg
cr.file: Fragments of the Colossus of Constantine, courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome.jpg
cr.line: Fragments of the Colossus of Constantine, courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY PEOPLE SUSPECT A COVER-UP
cards.body: The real process was slow, boring and spread over centuries. A secret vote at a famous council is a better story, so the invented version keeps beating the documented one.

cr.artwork: Codex Vaticanus B, 2Thess. 3,11-18, Hebr. 1,1-2,2.jpg
cr.file: Codex Vaticanus B, 2Thess. 3,11-18, Hebr. 1,1-2,2.jpg
cr.line: Codex Vaticanus B, 2Thess. 3,11-18, Hebr. 1,1-2,2.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Codex Sinaiticus, 4th century, the oldest surviving complete copy of the New Testament. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Alexander the Great's missing tomb
stacks.hook: Alexander the Great conquered one of the largest empires the world had ever seen by 32. Then he died, his empire collapsed, and eventually even his body disappeared.

cards.head: Alexander the Great conquered one of the largest empires the world had ever seen by 32.
cards.body: Then he died, his empire collapsed, and eventually even his body disappeared. Alexander's tomb became one of the most famous monuments of the ancient world. Today, nobody knows where it is.

cr.artwork: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic.jpg
cr.file: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic.jpg
cr.line: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE BECAME KING AT 20
cards.body: Alexander inherited Macedonia in 336 BCE after his father Philip II was assassinated. Within years, he launched an invasion of the enormous Persian Empire.

cr.artwork: Alexander the Great mosaic.jpg
cr.file: Alexander the Great mosaic.jpg
cr.line: Alexander the Great mosaic.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN HE BASICALLY DIDN'T STOP
cards.body: Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III and conquered territory stretching from Greece and Egypt through Persia and into parts of Central and South Asia. He founded cities, including Alexandria in Egypt, and became legendary before turning 30.

cr.artwork: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg
cr.file: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg
cr.line: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN AT 32, HE SUDDENLY DIED
cards.body: In 323 BCE, Alexander became ill in Babylon and died after days of worsening symptoms. Ancient sources offer competing explanations, and historians still debate exactly what killed him.

cr.artwork: Naval battles, ancient and modern (1883) (14764701592).jpg
cr.file: Naval battles, ancient and modern (1883) (14764701592).jpg
cr.line: Naval battles, ancient and modern (1883) (14764701592).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS GENERALS FOUGHT OVER EVERYTHING
cards.body: Alexander left no clear adult successor capable of controlling his empire. His generals eventually fought a series of wars and divided his territories among themselves.

cr.artwork: Alexander and Bucephalus G-002624.jpg
cr.file: Alexander and Bucephalus G-002624.jpg
cr.line: Alexander and Bucephalus G-002624.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EVEN HIS CORPSE BECAME POLITICAL
cards.body: Alexander's body was taken to Egypt and eventually placed in an elaborate tomb in Alexandria. Famous Romans including Julius Caesar and Augustus were later said to have visited it.

cr.artwork: Angelique Mongez - Mort de Darius.jpg
cr.file: Angelique Mongez - Mort de Darius.jpg
cr.line: Angelique Mongez - Mort de Darius.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND THEN THE TOMB VANISHED
cards.body: References to Alexander's tomb eventually disappear from the historical record as ancient Alexandria endured centuries of upheaval, earthquakes and reconstruction. Archaeologists have searched repeatedly, but the confirmed tomb and body of one of history's greatest conquerors have never been found.

cr.artwork: Alexandermosaic.jpg
cr.file: Alexandermosaic.jpg
cr.line: Alexandermosaic.jpg. Photo: Magrippa at English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE TOMB HUNT NEVER ENDS
cards.body: Egyptian authorities have recognised more than 140 official attempts to find it. Every one has failed, and each failure narrows the map just enough to justify the next.

cr.artwork: Alexander Sarcophagus, long side B, hunting scene, Istanbul Archaeology Museum (14042900900).jpg
cr.file: Alexander Sarcophagus, long side B, hunting scene, Istanbul Archaeology Museum (14042900900).jpg
cr.line: Alexander Sarcophagus, long side B, hunting scene, Istanbul Archaeology Museum (14042900900).jpg. Photo: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Joan of Arc
stacks.hook: Joan of Arc was a teenage peasant who said she heard voices from God. Somehow, within a few years, she was helping lead France to war.

cards.head: Joan of Arc was a teenage peasant who said she heard voices from God.
cards.body: Somehow, within a few years, she was helping lead France to war. She couldn't have known that before turning 20, she would help transform a war, be captured, tried for heresy and burned alive.

cr.artwork: Joan Parliament of Paris.png
cr.file: Joan Parliament of Paris.png
cr.line: Joan Parliament of Paris.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SHE SAID SAINTS SPOKE TO HER
cards.body: As a teenager, Joan said she received messages from saints including Michael, Catherine and Margaret. She believed God had given her a mission to help Charles VII and drive his enemies from France.

cr.artwork: Dante Gabriel Rossetti - Joan of Arc (1882).jpg
cr.file: Dante Gabriel Rossetti - Joan of Arc (1882).jpg
cr.line: Dante Gabriel Rossetti - Joan of Arc (1882).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOMEHOW SHE GOT THE FUTURE KING TO LISTEN
cards.body: At around 17, Joan traveled to meet Charles and convinced his court to take her seriously. She was eventually allowed to accompany French forces attempting to relieve the besieged city of Orléans.

cr.artwork: Ingres coronation charles vii.jpg
cr.file: Ingres coronation charles vii.jpg
cr.line: Ingres coronation charles vii.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND THEN THEY STARTED WINNING
cards.body: The siege of Orléans was lifted in 1429, turning Joan into a sensation. French forces subsequently won further victories, and Charles was crowned king at Reims with Joan present.

cr.artwork: L.-M. Boutet de Monvel - Joan of Arc during the siege of Tournelles, 7 May 1429.png
cr.file: L.-M. Boutet de Monvel - Joan of Arc during the siege of Tournelles, 7 May 1429.png
cr.line: L.-M. Boutet de Monvel - Joan of Arc during the siege of Tournelles, 7 May 1429.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN SHE WAS CAPTURED
cards.body: In 1430, Joan was captured by Burgundian forces allied with the English. She was eventually transferred to the English, who supported a church trial accusing her of heresy.

cr.artwork: Jules Bastien-Lepage Johanna von Orleans anagoria.JPG
cr.file: Jules Bastien-Lepage Johanna von Orleans anagoria.JPG
cr.line: Jules Bastien-Lepage Johanna von Orleans anagoria.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEY BURNED HER ALIVE
cards.body: Joan was convicted and burned at the stake in Rouen in 1431. She was approximately 19 years old.

cr.artwork: JoanOfArcLarge.jpeg
cr.file: JoanOfArcLarge.jpeg
cr.line: JoanOfArcLarge.jpeg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN THE CHURCH REVERSED THE VERDICT
cards.body: Twenty-five years later, a new church proceeding overturned the original judgment and declared the trial deeply flawed. Nearly five centuries after her execution, the Catholic Church canonized Joan of Arc as a saint.

cr.artwork: Agnès Sorel - anonyme XVIe.jpg
cr.file: Agnès Sorel - anonyme XVIe.jpg
cr.line: Agnès Sorel - anonyme XVIe.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY EVERY SIDE CLAIMS HER
cards.body: A teenage girl who won battles and was executed by a church court can be a saint, a nationalist, a feminist or a martyr. She has been used as all four, often at the same time.

cr.artwork: Joan of Arc MET DP-14201-049.jpg
cr.file: Joan of Arc MET DP-14201-049.jpg
cr.line: Joan of Arc MET DP-14201-049.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Satan does not rule Hell
stacks.hook: Satan does not rule Hell. In the Bible, Hell is actually part of his punishment.

cards.head: Satan does not rule Hell.
cards.body: In the Bible, Hell is actually part of his punishment. The popular image of Satan sitting on a throne commanding demons in Hell owes more to later art and literature than the biblical text. Revelation describes Satan eventually being thrown into the lake of fire himself.

cr.artwork: Satan Exulting over Eve.jpg
cr.file: Satan Exulting over Eve.jpg
cr.line: Satan Exulting over Eve.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SATAN STARTS AS AN ENEMY, NOT A KING
cards.body: In Christian theology, Satan is a created spiritual being who rebels against God. He is never presented as an evil god with power equal to God's.
cards.cap: scanned, post-processed, and uploaded by Karl Hahn. Paul Gustave Doré, 1832-1883 (artist);

cr.artwork: DVinfernoLuciferKingOfHell m.jpg
cr.file: DVinfernoLuciferKingOfHell m.jpg
cr.credit: scanned, post-processed, and uploaded by Karl Hahn. Paul Gustave Doré, 1832-1883 (artist);
cr.line: DVinfernoLuciferKingOfHell m.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE IS ACTUALLY ASSOCIATED WITH EARTH
cards.body: The New Testament describes Satan as actively tempting and deceiving people in the world. First Peter even compares him to a roaring lion roaming around looking for someone to devour.

cr.artwork: Pieter Bruegel I-Fall of rebel Angels (merge).jpg
cr.file: Pieter Bruegel I-Fall of rebel Angels (merge).jpg
cr.line: Pieter Bruegel I-Fall of rebel Angels (merge).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EVEN HIS POWER HAS LIMITS
cards.body: The Book of Job portrays "the satan" acting only within boundaries permitted by God. The basic biblical framework is not two equal supernatural powers fighting for control.

cr.artwork: Cloisters Apocalypse - Dragon and the Beasts cast into Hell.jpg
cr.file: Cloisters Apocalypse - Dragon and the Beasts cast into Hell.jpg
cr.line: Cloisters Apocalypse - Dragon and the Beasts cast into Hell.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN REVELATION DESCRIBES HIS DEFEAT
cards.body: Revelation depicts Satan as a dragon who wages war against God's people. Eventually, he is defeated and imprisoned.

cr.artwork: Inferno Canto 34 (148619628).jpg
cr.file: Inferno Canto 34 (148619628).jpg
cr.line: Inferno Canto 34 (148619628).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN SATAN IS THROWN INTO THE LAKE OF FIRE
cards.body: Revelation 20 says Satan is thrown into the lake of fire, where he is tormented. He isn't running the place. He's being punished there.

cr.artwork: GuidoReni MichaelDefeatsSatan.jpg
cr.file: GuidoReni MichaelDefeatsSatan.jpg
cr.line: GuidoReni MichaelDefeatsSatan.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO WHO RULES HELL?
cards.body: Biblically, Hell isn't Satan's rival kingdom where he punishes bad people on God's behalf. The familiar image developed through centuries of theology, literature and art, while the biblical Satan ultimately faces judgment himself.

cr.artwork: Gottliche Komodie. T. 1, Die Holle 1870 (148619628).jpg
cr.file: Gottliche Komodie. T. 1, Die Holle 1870 (148619628).jpg
cr.line: Gottliche Komodie. T. 1, Die Holle 1870 (148619628).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE POPULAR HELL IS NOT THE BIBLICAL ONE
cards.body: The throne, the pitchfork and the underworld kingdom come from Dante and Milton. Literature drew it more vividly than scripture did, and the vivid version is the one that stuck.

cr.artwork: Morozov Apocalypse (c.1820, Christie's) Attack.jpg
cr.file: Morozov Apocalypse (c.1820, Christie's) Attack.jpg
cr.line: Morozov Apocalypse (c.1820, Christie's) Attack.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.cap: William Blake, Satan Exulting over Eve, c. 1795, Tate Britain

cr.artwork: William Blake, Satan Exulting over Eve, c. 1795, Tate Britain
cr.line: William Blake, Satan Exulting over Eve, c. 1795, Tate Britain. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Biblical creatures look nothing like paintings
stacks.hook: The Bible describes creatures that look nothing like the angels you see in paintings.

cards.head: The Bible describes creatures that look nothing like the angels you see in paintings.
cards.body: The familiar beautiful human with two white wings is only one artistic tradition. Some biblical heavenly beings are described with multiple faces, enormous wings and bodies covered in eyes.

cr.artwork: Giuseppe Cades (1750-1799) - Vision of Ezekiel (copy after Raphael) - 03-1184 - Royal Academy of Arts.jpg
cr.file: Giuseppe Cades (1750-1799) - Vision of Ezekiel (copy after Raphael) - 03-1184 - Royal Academy of Arts.jpg
cr.line: Giuseppe Cades (1750-1799) - Vision of Ezekiel (copy after Raphael) - 03-1184 - Royal Academy of Arts.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: CHERUBIM ARE NOT BABIES
cards.body: Today, cherubs are often depicted as chubby winged infants. But Ezekiel describes cherubim as terrifying beings with four faces, including those of a human, lion, ox and eagle.

cr.artwork: Raffael-vision-ezechiel.jpg
cr.file: Raffael-vision-ezechiel.jpg
cr.line: Raffael-vision-ezechiel.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN THERE ARE SERAPHIM
cards.body: Isaiah sees beings called seraphim surrounding God's throne. Each has six wings: two covering its face, two covering its feet and two used to fly.
cards.cap: Pieter van Aelst (Pieter van Edingen)'s workshop, Brussels. Cartoon by Tommaso Vincidor ba

cr.artwork: La visión de Ezequiel (Pieter van Aelst).jpg
cr.file: La visión de Ezequiel (Pieter van Aelst).jpg
cr.credit: Pieter van Aelst (Pieter van Edingen)'s workshop, Brussels. Cartoon by Tommaso Vincidor ba
cr.line: La visión de Ezequiel (Pieter van Aelst).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EZEKIEL SEES WHEELS COVERED IN EYES
cards.body: Ezekiel describes mysterious intersecting wheels moving alongside the heavenly creatures. Their rims are described as being full of eyes.

cr.artwork: KellsFol027v4Evang.jpg
cr.file: KellsFol027v4Evang.jpg
cr.line: KellsFol027v4Evang.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT SOME ANGELS LOOK COMPLETELY HUMAN
cards.body: Not every biblical angel is bizarre-looking. Angels frequently appear as men, sometimes so normally that people don't immediately realize they're encountering supernatural beings.

cr.artwork: Ridpath's Universal history - an account of the origin, primitive condition and ethnic development of the great races of mankind, and of the principal events in the evolution and progress of the (14782047134).jpg
cr.file: Ridpath's Universal history - an account of the origin, primitive condition and ethnic development of the great races of mankind, and of the principal events in the evolution and progress of the (14782047134).jpg
cr.line: Ridpath's Universal history - an account of the origin, primitive condition and ethnic development of the great races of mankind, and of the principal events in the evolution and progress of the (14782047134).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: "BE NOT AFRAID" IS MORE COMPLICATED
cards.body: The internet joke says angels constantly introduce themselves by saying "do not be afraid" because they look terrifying. Angels do reassure frightened humans in the Bible, but the text doesn't say it's specifically because their appearance is horrifying.

cr.artwork: Angel Nikea.jpg
cr.file: Angel Nikea.jpg
cr.line: Angel Nikea.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: "ANGEL" IS ACTUALLY A JOB DESCRIPTION
cards.body: The biblical words translated as "angel" essentially mean messenger. Cherubim, seraphim and other heavenly beings aren't necessarily interchangeable species of what modern culture calls angels.

cr.artwork: Montauban - L'église St Jacques - Mosaïque.jpg
cr.file: Montauban - L'église St Jacques - Mosaïque.jpg
cr.line: Montauban - L'église St Jacques - Mosaïque.jpg. Photo: Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE REAL DESCRIPTIONS SHOCK PEOPLE
cards.body: Most people meet angels through Renaissance painting first and the text second. Finding out the source material describes something far stranger feels like a revelation, though it was never hidden.

cr.artwork: William Blake Ezekiel's Vision ca 1803-5 Boston Museum.jpg
cr.file: William Blake Ezekiel's Vision ca 1803-5 Boston Museum.jpg
cr.line: William Blake Ezekiel's Vision ca 1803-5 Boston Museum.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Raphael, The Vision of Ezekiel, c. 1518, Palazzo Pitti, Florence. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Jesus's brothers and sisters
stacks.hook: The Bible says Jesus had brothers and sisters. So who were they?

cards.head: The Bible says Jesus had brothers and sisters.
cards.body: So who were they? The Gospels explicitly mention Jesus's brothers James, Joseph, Judas and Simon and say he had sisters. What Christians have debated for centuries is what exactly "brothers and sisters" means.

cr.artwork: James the Just (Novgorod, 16 c.).jpg
cr.file: James the Just (Novgorod, 16 c.).jpg
cr.line: James the Just (Novgorod, 16 c.).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: MARK ACTUALLY NAMES THEM
cards.body: In Mark 6, people in Jesus's hometown identify him as Mary's son and name four brothers. His sisters are mentioned too, although their names aren't given.

cr.artwork: Andrea Mantegna (workshop) Holy Family.jpg
cr.file: Andrea Mantegna (workshop) Holy Family.jpg
cr.line: Andrea Mantegna (workshop) Holy Family.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AT FIRST, HIS FAMILY DIDN'T SEEM CONVINCED
cards.body: The Gospels contain surprisingly tense moments involving Jesus's family. John even states that at one point his brothers did not believe in him.

cr.artwork: Saint Christopher Carrying the Christ Child - Limbourg Brothers - NGA.jpg
cr.file: Saint Christopher Carrying the Christ Child - Limbourg Brothers - NGA.jpg
cr.line: Saint Christopher Carrying the Christ Child - Limbourg Brothers - NGA.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN SOMETHING CHANGED
cards.body: After Jesus's death, his brother James emerges as one of the most important leaders of the Jerusalem Christian community. Paul specifically describes meeting "James, the Lord's brother."
cards.cap: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope from Greenbelt, MD, USA

cr.artwork: James Webb Tours the Manned Space Center (45052591872).jpg
cr.file: James Webb Tours the Manned Space Center (45052591872).jpg
cr.credit: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope from Greenbelt, MD, USA
cr.line: James Webb Tours the Manned Space Center (45052591872).jpg. Photo: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope from Greenbelt, MD, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WERE THEY MARY'S OTHER CHILDREN?
cards.body: Many Protestants interpret the passages straightforwardly as younger children of Mary and Joseph. That would make them Jesus's biological half-siblings.

cr.artwork: On Nazareth hill (1915) (14761720336).jpg
cr.file: On Nazareth hill (1915) (14761720336).jpg
cr.line: On Nazareth hill (1915) (14761720336).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: CATHOLICS AND ORTHODOX CHRISTIANS INTERPRET IT DIFFERENTLY
cards.body: Catholic tradition generally understands them as close relatives rather than Mary's biological children, while an ancient Eastern Christian tradition identifies them as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. These interpretations preserve the doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.

cr.artwork: Andrea mantegna, sacra famiglia con san giovannino, 1500 ca. 01.jpg
cr.file: Andrea mantegna, sacra famiglia con san giovannino, 1500 ca. 01.jpg
cr.line: Andrea mantegna, sacra famiglia con san giovannino, 1500 ca. 01.jpg. Photo: Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WE DON'T ACTUALLY KNOW
cards.body: The New Testament clearly identifies people as Jesus's brothers and sisters but doesn't explain the precise family relationship in modern terms. What is clear is that at least one of them, James, became enormously important after Jesus's death.
cards.cap: Anonymous Russian icon painter (before 1917)Public domain image (according to PD-Russi

cr.file: Menaion icon (17 c., TsAK) - October.jpg
cr.credit: Anonymous Russian icon painter (before 1917)Public domain image (according to PD-Russi
cr.line: Menaion icon (17 c., TsAK) - October.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THIS DETAIL STAYS AWKWARD
cards.body: The text says one thing and centuries of doctrine say another, and both are still in circulation. Questions that different traditions answer differently do not fade, they get inherited.

cr.file: Saints Iacov, Flor, and Lavr. State Russian Museum. St. Petersburg.jpg
cr.line: Saints Iacov, Flor, and Lavr. State Russian Museum. St. Petersburg.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: What happened to Pontius Pilate?
stacks.hook: The man who sentenced Jesus to death basically disappears from the Bible immediately afterward. So what happened to Pontius Pilate?

cards.head: The man who sentenced Jesus to death basically disappears from the Bible immediately afterward.
cards.body: So what happened to Pontius Pilate? Pilate governed Judea for roughly a decade and ordered one of history's most famous executions. Then his own political career ended under strange circumstances.

cr.artwork: Caesarea maritima BW 5.JPG
cr.file: Caesarea maritima BW 5.JPG
cr.line: Caesarea maritima BW 5.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: PILATE WAS ROME'S GOVERNOR
cards.body: Pontius Pilate governed Judea under Emperor Tiberius from about 26 to 36 CE. Ancient Jewish writers portray him as a harsh administrator who repeatedly clashed with the people he governed.

cr.artwork: Antonio Ciseri - Ecce Homo.jpg
cr.file: Antonio Ciseri - Ecce Homo.jpg
cr.line: Antonio Ciseri - Ecce Homo.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE AUTHORIZED JESUS'S CRUCIFIXION
cards.body: All four canonical Gospels place Jesus before Pilate. Whatever differences exist between their accounts, Roman authority ultimately imposed the crucifixion.

cr.artwork: Brugghen Pilate washing his hands 01.jpg
cr.file: Brugghen Pilate washing his hands 01.jpg
cr.line: Brugghen Pilate washing his hands 01.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: PILATE KEPT GETTING INTO TROUBLE
cards.body: The Jewish writers Josephus and Philo describe controversies involving Roman standards, Temple funds and violence under Pilate. His governorship appears considerably harsher than the hesitant figure emphasized in some Gospel scenes.

cr.artwork: Dedicatory inscription found reused in the staircase of the theatre of Caesarea, the first and only mention of Pontius Pilates' name ever unearthed, 26-36 AD, Israel Museum, Jerusalem (15655925251).jpg

cards.head: THEN A MASSACRE ENDED HIS CAREER
cards.body: According to Josephus, Pilate's forces attacked a gathering of Samaritans after a man promised to reveal sacred objects on Mount Gerizim. Samaritan leaders complained to Pilate's superior.

cards.head: ROME ORDERED HIM HOME
cards.body: Pilate was ordered to Rome to answer accusations about his conduct. By the time he arrived, Emperor Tiberius had died.

cards.head: THEN HISTORY LOSES HIM
cards.body: Reliable ancient evidence doesn't tell us what happened to Pilate afterward. Later Christian legends gave him wildly different endings, from suicide to conversion, but his actual fate remains unknown.

cr.file: Jerusalem Modell BW 4.JPG

cards.head: WHY PILATE KEEPS HIS ROLE
cards.body: He is named in the creed millions recite weekly, which makes him the only Roman official most people can name. A stone from Caesarea is the only contemporary proof he existed.

stacks.title: The Book of Enoch
stacks.hook: The Book of Enoch describes fallen angels, giants and forbidden knowledge. So why isn't it in most Bibles?

cards.head: The Book of Enoch describes fallen angels, giants and forbidden knowledge.
cards.body: So why isn't it in most Bibles? Enoch was enormously influential in ancient Judaism and early Christianity. The New Testament's Letter of Jude even quotes material found in it.

cr.artwork: BL Or 485 f. 102r.png
cr.file: BL Or 485 f. 102r.png
cr.line: BL Or 485 f. 102r.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: IT EXPANDS ONE OF GENESIS'S WEIRDEST STORIES
cards.body: Genesis briefly describes mysterious "sons of God" having children with human women, producing the Nephilim. First Enoch turns this tiny passage into an enormous story.

cr.artwork: Annunciation to Zechariah British Library Add. MS 59874 Ethiopian Bible.jpg
cr.file: Annunciation to Zechariah British Library Add. MS 59874 Ethiopian Bible.jpg
cr.line: Annunciation to Zechariah British Library Add. MS 59874 Ethiopian Bible.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: ANGELS COME DOWN TO EARTH
cards.body: In Enoch, angels called Watchers descend to Earth and take human wives. They also teach humanity forbidden knowledge involving weapons, magic and other arts.

cr.artwork: Ethiopian, Illuminated Manuscript, 18th century.jpg
cr.file: Ethiopian, Illuminated Manuscript, 18th century.jpg
cr.line: Ethiopian, Illuminated Manuscript, 18th century.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEIR CHILDREN BECOME GIANTS
cards.body: The unions produce violent giants who devastate the Earth. Their corruption becomes part of the explanation for the wickedness preceding Noah's flood.

cr.artwork: Paradise Lost 1.jpg
cr.file: Paradise Lost 1.jpg
cr.line: Paradise Lost 1.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: GOD PUNISHES THE WATCHERS
cards.body: The rebellious angels are bound and await judgment. Enoch himself becomes a visionary who is shown heavenly mysteries and coming divine judgment.
cards.cap: Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (839–923)

cr.file: Adam and the Angels watched by Iblis.jpg
cr.credit: Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (839–923)
cr.line: Adam and the Angels watched by Iblis.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EARLY CHRISTIANS KNEW THIS BOOK
cards.body: Jude contains a passage closely corresponding to 1 Enoch and explicitly attributes the prophecy to Enoch. The book's ideas also influenced early Jewish and Christian thinking about fallen angels.

cr.artwork: Oxford, Sackler Library MS P.Oxy. XXXIV 2684 (Papyrus 78) recto Jude 1, 4; 1, 8.jpg
cr.file: Oxford, Sackler Library MS P.Oxy. XXXIV 2684 (Papyrus 78) recto Jude 1, 4; 1, 8.jpg

cards.head: ONE MAJOR CHRISTIAN TRADITION STILL HAS IT
cards.body: First Enoch did not become part of the Jewish or most Christian biblical canons. But the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church preserved it as Scripture, which is one reason the complete work survived.

cr.artwork: Aethiopisch orthodoxer Moench.jpg
cr.file: Aethiopisch orthodoxer Moench.jpg
cr.line: Aethiopisch orthodoxer Moench.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY A BANNED BOOK GETS READ
cards.body: Enoch was influential enough to be quoted in the New Testament and still left out of most Bibles. Anything excluded after being taken seriously acquires an appeal that inclusion would have killed.

stacks.title: What killed Alexander the Great?
stacks.hook: Alexander the Great died at 32, and nobody can agree on what killed him.

cards.head: Alexander the Great died at 32, and nobody can agree on what killed him.
cards.body: After conquering an empire stretching thousands of miles, Alexander returned to Babylon in 323 BCE. Then he developed a fever, deteriorated for days and died.

cr.artwork: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg
cr.file: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg
cr.line: Alexandre, l'Iponos - musée du Louvre.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE HAD JUST RETURNED TO BABYLON
cards.body: Alexander was planning new military campaigns when he became seriously ill. Ancient accounts describe his condition worsening over roughly a week or more.

cr.artwork: Idealized head of Alexander the Great called "Alexander Guimet", Louvre Museum (7462976260).jpg
cr.file: Idealized head of Alexander the Great called "Alexander Guimet", Louvre Museum (7462976260).jpg
cr.line: Idealized head of Alexander the Great called "Alexander Guimet", Louvre Museum (7462976260).jpg. Photo: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE EVENTUALLY COULDN'T SPEAK
cards.body: One tradition says Alexander's soldiers filed past his bed as he lay dying. Unable to speak, he acknowledged them with his eyes or a slight movement.
cards.cap: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division Washington, D.C. 20540 USA

cr.artwork: Ishtar-gate-بوابة-عشتار.jpg
cr.file: Ishtar-gate-بوابة-عشتار.jpg
cr.credit: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division Washington, D.C. 20540 USA
cr.line: Ishtar-gate-بوابة-عشتار.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: NATURAL DISEASE IS A MAJOR POSSIBILITY
cards.body: Modern theories have proposed illnesses including typhoid fever and other infections. Diagnosing a man who died more than 2,300 years ago from literary descriptions is inherently uncertain.

cr.artwork: Alexander Runciman (1736-1785) - The Death of Dido - NG 2543 - National Galleries of Scotland.jpg
cr.file: Alexander Runciman (1736-1785) - The Death of Dido - NG 2543 - National Galleries of Scotland.jpg
cr.line: Alexander Runciman (1736-1785) - The Death of Dido - NG 2543 - National Galleries of Scotland.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT PEOPLE IMMEDIATELY SUSPECTED POISON
cards.body: Ancient stories also claimed Alexander had been poisoned. Modern historians generally treat the dramatic poisoning traditions cautiously, particularly because the reported illness lasted for days.

cr.artwork: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic.jpg
cr.file: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic.jpg
cr.line: Alexander (Battle of Issus) Mosaic.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN CAME AN EVEN STRANGER STORY
cards.body: One ancient tradition claimed Alexander's body didn't begin decomposing for several days, which was interpreted as proof of his divinity. Modern attempts to diagnose him from that story are speculative.
cards.cap: Ángel M. Felicísimo from Mérida, España

cr.artwork: Alejandro Magno (26767375975).jpg
cr.file: Alejandro Magno (26767375975).jpg
cr.credit: Ángel M. Felicísimo from Mérida, España
cr.line: Alejandro Magno (26767375975).jpg. Photo: Ángel M. Felicísimo from Mérida, España, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS DEATH CREATED ANOTHER DISASTER
cards.body: Alexander had no undisputed adult heir ready to inherit the empire. His commanders eventually tore his territories apart fighting over who would control what he had conquered.

cr.artwork: Bust of Alexander the Great, Found on Island of Delos, c. 2nd C. BC (27687211503).jpg
cr.file: Bust of Alexander the Great, Found on Island of Delos, c. 2nd C. BC (27687211503).jpg
cr.line: Bust of Alexander the Great, Found on Island of Delos, c. 2nd C. BC (27687211503).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE CAUSE STAYS OPEN
cards.body: Fever, poisoning and disease all still fit the surviving descriptions, and no body exists to test. A question that cannot be closed keeps getting reopened.

cr.artwork: Minerva Alexander Mazarin Louvre Ma3385.jpg
cr.file: Minerva Alexander Mazarin Louvre Ma3385.jpg
cr.line: Minerva Alexander Mazarin Louvre Ma3385.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
