stacks.title: Napoleon wasn't short
stacks.hook: Napoleon wasn't actually short. So why does basically everyone think he was?

cards.head: Napoleon wasn't actually short.
cards.body: So why does basically everyone think he was? Napoleon is remembered as the tiny emperor compensating for his height by conquering Europe. The historical Napoleon was probably around average height for a Frenchman of his era.

cr.artwork: Ingres, Napoleon on his Imperial throne.jpg
cr.file: Ingres, Napoleon on his Imperial throne.jpg
cr.line: Ingres, Napoleon on his Imperial throne.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE CONFUSION STARTS WITH HIS RECORDED HEIGHT
cards.body: After Napoleon's death, his height was recorded as five feet two inches in French measurements. French inches were longer than British inches, making that roughly five feet six or seven in modern imperial measurement.

cr.artwork: English Caricaturists, 1893 - Gillray Boney 3.png
cr.file: English Caricaturists, 1893 - Gillray Boney 3.png
cr.line: English Caricaturists, 1893 - Gillray Boney 3.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN BRITAIN TURNED HIM INTO A CARICATURE
cards.body: Britain was Napoleon's enemy, and British cartoonists repeatedly portrayed him as tiny. James Gillray's enormously influential caricatures helped cement the image.

cr.artwork: Bonaparte David Charlottenburg.jpg
cr.file: Bonaparte David Charlottenburg.jpg
cr.line: Bonaparte David Charlottenburg.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EVEN HIS NICKNAME SOUNDS SUSPICIOUS
cards.body: Napoleon was known as "Le Petit Caporal," or "the Little Corporal." But the nickname was affectionate and referred more to his relationship with soldiers than necessarily to his physical height.

cr.artwork: Hippolyte Paul Delaroche (1797-1856) - Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) crossing the Alps - RCIN 404874 - Royal Collection.jpg
cr.file: Hippolyte Paul Delaroche (1797-1856) - Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) crossing the Alps - RCIN 404874 - Royal Collection.jpg
cr.line: Hippolyte Paul Delaroche (1797-1856) - Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) crossing the Alps - RCIN 404874 - Royal Collection.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS GUARDS ALSO MADE HIM LOOK SMALLER
cards.body: Napoleon surrounded himself with Imperial Guards who had height requirements and were often notably tall. Standing beside them could make an average-height man appear smaller.

cr.artwork: Napoleon with 2 wives - collage by shakko.jpg
cr.file: Napoleon with 2 wives - collage by shakko.jpg
cr.line: Napoleon with 2 wives - collage by shakko.jpg. Photo: shakko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN THE MYTH OUTLIVED THE MAN
cards.body: The image became so powerful that "Napoleon complex" eventually became shorthand for supposedly aggressive behavior by short men. Napoleon's name became attached to a psychological stereotype built partly on a false premise.

cr.artwork: Paris, Les Invalides, Tombeau De Napoleon. (111-76)-Paris, Les Invalides, Tombeau De Napoleon.... (NBY 418090).jpg
cr.file: Paris, Les Invalides, Tombeau De Napoleon. (111-76)-Paris, Les Invalides, Tombeau De Napoleon.... (NBY 418090).jpg
cr.line: Paris, Les Invalides, Tombeau De Napoleon. (111-76)-Paris, Les Invalides, Tombeau De Napoleon.... (NBY 418090).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: PROPAGANDA WON
cards.body: Napoleon conquered much of Europe, crowned himself emperor and reshaped European politics. Yet one of the most persistent facts people remember about him is something that probably wasn't true.

cr.artwork: Bodleian Libraries, Maniac Ravings or - Little Boney in a strong fit.jpg
cr.file: Bodleian Libraries, Maniac Ravings or - Little Boney in a strong fit.jpg
cr.line: Bodleian Libraries, Maniac Ravings or - Little Boney in a strong fit.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE SHORT MYTH REFUSES TO DIE
cards.body: It is now a term used in psychology. Once a mistake becomes a word for a personality type, correcting the history no longer touches the belief.

cr.file: Bodleian Libraries, The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver.jpg
cr.line: Bodleian Libraries, The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Joan of Arc's trial reversed
stacks.hook: Joan of Arc was burned alive for heresy. Twenty-five years later, the Church basically admitted the trial was wrong.

cards.head: Joan of Arc was burned alive for heresy.
cards.body: Twenty-five years later, the Church basically admitted the trial was wrong. Joan died at around 19 after helping change the course of the Hundred Years' War. Her story didn't end with her execution.

cr.artwork: Dante Gabriel Rossetti - Joan of Arc (1882).jpg
cr.file: Dante Gabriel Rossetti - Joan of Arc (1882).jpg
cr.line: Dante Gabriel Rossetti - Joan of Arc (1882).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HER ENEMIES NEEDED TO DISCREDIT HER
cards.body: Joan claimed God had commanded her to support Charles VII's claim to the French throne. If she really was God's messenger, that gave Charles's cause enormous religious legitimacy.

cr.artwork: JoanOfArcLarge.jpeg
cr.file: JoanOfArcLarge.jpeg
cr.line: JoanOfArcLarge.jpeg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO THEY PUT HER ON TRIAL
cards.body: After Joan was captured, she was tried by an ecclesiastical court operating under strong English influence. She faced accusations involving her visions, religious authority and wearing men's clothing.

cr.artwork: Claude Monet - Rouen Cathedral, Facade (Sunset).JPG
cr.file: Claude Monet - Rouen Cathedral, Facade (Sunset).JPG
cr.line: Claude Monet - Rouen Cathedral, Facade (Sunset).JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SHE WAS CONDEMNED
cards.body: After months of interrogation, Joan was convicted of heresy. On May 30, 1431, she was burned at the stake in Rouen.
cards.cap: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress

cr.artwork: Entrance to cathedral of Reims, France, and equestrian statue of Joan of Arc LCCN2002699879.jpg
cr.file: Entrance to cathedral of Reims, France, and equestrian statue of Joan of Arc LCCN2002699879.jpg
cr.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress
cr.line: Entrance to cathedral of Reims, France, and equestrian statue of Joan of Arc LCCN2002699879.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN HER SIDE WON
cards.body: The Hundred Years' War continued, but French fortunes improved dramatically. Charles VII ultimately secured his position, while England lost nearly all of its French territories.

cr.artwork: Joan Parliament of Paris.png
cr.file: Joan Parliament of Paris.png
cr.line: Joan Parliament of Paris.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HER CASE WAS REOPENED
cards.body: Decades after Joan's death, a new investigation examined the original proceedings. In 1456, the earlier conviction was annulled and Joan was declared innocent of the charges that had condemned her.

cr.artwork: Agnès Sorel - anonyme XVIe.jpg
cr.file: Agnès Sorel - anonyme XVIe.jpg
cr.line: Agnès Sorel - anonyme XVIe.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN SHE BECAME A SAINT
cards.body: In 1920, nearly five centuries after she was burned as a heretic, the Catholic Church canonized Joan of Arc. The teenager once condemned by a church court became one of Catholicism's most famous saints.
cards.cap: Agence de presse Meurisse. Agence photographique (commanditaire)

cr.line: La canonisation de Jeanne d'Arc à Rome - arrivée des pélerins à Saint Pierre de Rome - btv1b9033716b.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE REVERSAL MATTERS MORE THAN THE TRIAL
cards.body: A court that convicts and a court that later admits it was wrong is a rare sequence. The retrial is why she is a saint rather than a footnote.

stacks.title: Nero didn't fiddle while Rome burned
stacks.hook: Nero probably didn't fiddle while Rome burned. For one thing, the violin wouldn't exist for another thousand years.

cards.head: Nero probably didn't fiddle while Rome burned.
cards.body: For one thing, the violin wouldn't exist for another thousand years. The story that Emperor Nero casually played music while Rome burned in 64 CE became shorthand for cruel, incompetent leadership. The real history is more complicated.

cr.artwork: Foxe's Christian martyrs of the world; the story of the advance of Christianity from Bible times to latest periods of persecution (1907) (14760870866).jpg
cr.file: Foxe's Christian martyrs of the world; the story of the advance of Christianity from Bible times to latest periods of persecution (1907) (14760870866).jpg
cr.line: Foxe's Christian martyrs of the world; the story of the advance of Christianity from Bible times to latest periods of persecution (1907) (14760870866).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: ROME REALLY DID BURN
cards.body: A catastrophic fire broke out in July 64 CE and burned for days. Large sections of Rome were destroyed, leaving enormous numbers of residents homeless.

cr.artwork: Fire in Rome.jpg
cr.file: Fire in Rome.jpg
cr.line: Fire in Rome.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: NERO PROBABLY WASN'T EVEN THERE WHEN IT STARTED
cards.body: The Roman historian Tacitus says Nero was at Antium when the fire began. He returned to Rome and opened public spaces to displaced residents.

cr.artwork: Civil war and rebellion in the Roman empire A.D. 69-70; companion to the "Histories" of Tacitus (1908) (14576214397).jpg
cr.file: Civil war and rebellion in the Roman empire A.D. 69-70; companion to the "Histories" of Tacitus (1908) (14576214397).jpg
cr.line: Civil war and rebellion in the Roman empire A.D. 69-70; companion to the "Histories" of Tacitus (1908) (14576214397).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT THERE WAS A TERRIBLE RUMOR
cards.body: Tacitus reports a rumor that Nero performed a song about the destruction of Troy while Rome burned. Whether that actually happened is unclear.
cards.cap: Unknown authorUnknown author, Ufficio Stampa Parco Archeologico Del Colosseo

cr.artwork: Centaur - Sala della Sfinge - Domus aurea - Rome.jpg
cr.file: Centaur - Sala della Sfinge - Domus aurea - Rome.jpg
cr.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Ufficio Stampa Parco Archeologico Del Colosseo
cr.line: Centaur - Sala della Sfinge - Domus aurea - Rome.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN NERO BUILT AN ENORMOUS PALACE
cards.body: After the fire, Nero constructed his extravagant Domus Aurea, or Golden House, across a large area of Rome. That helped fuel suspicions that he had benefited from the destruction.

cr.artwork: Martyrdom-of-Nagasaki-Painting-1622.png
cr.file: Martyrdom-of-Nagasaki-Painting-1622.png
cr.line: Martyrdom-of-Nagasaki-Painting-1622.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE NEEDED SOMEONE TO BLAME
cards.body: Tacitus says Nero blamed Christians for the fire and subjected them to horrific punishments. Some were reportedly crucified or burned to provide nighttime illumination.

cr.artwork: Balchik - The sanctuary of Cybele.JPG
cr.file: Balchik - The sanctuary of Cybele.JPG
cr.line: Balchik - The sanctuary of Cybele.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE LEGEND GOT BETTER THAN THE FACTS
cards.body: Centuries later, the story became "Nero fiddled while Rome burned." The fiddle is an anachronism, and whether Nero performed at all remains uncertain, but the phrase became immortal.
cards.cap: Tacitus (text copied by a monk in the 11th century). Photographic facsimile by Henricus Ro

cards.head: WHY WE WANT NERO AT THE WINDOW
cards.body: An emperor who does nothing while a city burns is a clean image of bad leadership. It is invoked constantly precisely because it is simple, and it is simple because it is not true.

stacks.title: The emperor who converted
stacks.hook: The Roman Empire spent centuries persecuting Christians. Then a Roman emperor converted, and everything changed.

cards.head: The Roman Empire spent centuries persecuting Christians.
cards.body: Then a Roman emperor converted, and everything changed. In the early fourth century, Christianity went from a periodically persecuted religion to one favored by the most powerful ruler in the Roman world.

cr.artwork: Fragments of the Colossus of Constantine, courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome.jpg
cr.file: Fragments of the Colossus of Constantine, courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome.jpg
cr.line: Fragments of the Colossus of Constantine, courtyard of the Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: FIRST CAME ONE OF THE WORST PERSECUTIONS
cards.body: Beginning in 303 CE, Emperor Diocletian and his colleagues ordered churches destroyed, Scriptures surrendered and Christians to comply with traditional Roman religious practices. The intensity varied dramatically across the empire.

cr.artwork: Arch Constantine reliefs, Rome, Italy.jpg
cr.file: Arch Constantine reliefs, Rome, Italy.jpg
cr.line: Arch Constantine reliefs, Rome, Italy.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN CONSTANTINE FOUGHT FOR THE EMPIRE
cards.body: After years of political chaos, Constantine fought his rival Maxentius for control of the western empire. Their decisive confrontation came at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome in 312.

cr.artwork: Battle at Pont Milvius.jpg
cr.file: Battle at Pont Milvius.jpg
cr.line: Battle at Pont Milvius.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: CONSTANTINE SAID HE RECEIVED A DIVINE SIGN
cards.body: Christian writers describe Constantine experiencing a vision or dream connected with the Christian God before the battle. He ordered a Christian-associated symbol placed on his soldiers' equipment.

cr.artwork: First Council of Nicaea Michael Damaskinos.png
cr.file: First Council of Nicaea Michael Damaskinos.png
cr.line: First Council of Nicaea Michael Damaskinos.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND THEN HE WON
cards.body: Maxentius was defeated and drowned during the battle. Constantine entered Rome victorious and increasingly associated himself with Christianity.

cr.artwork: Detail Constantine's Arch Round relief Rome 1.jpg
cr.file: Detail Constantine's Arch Round relief Rome 1.jpg
cr.line: Detail Constantine's Arch Round relief Rome 1.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: CHRISTIANITY BECAME LEGAL
cards.body: In 313, Constantine and Licinius issued an agreement granting religious toleration and restoring confiscated Christian property. Christianity was not yet the empire's official religion, but its political position had changed dramatically.

cr.artwork: Battle of the Milvian Bridge by Giulio Romano, 1520-24.jpg
cr.file: Battle of the Milvian Bridge by Giulio Romano, 1520-24.jpg
cr.line: Battle of the Milvian Bridge by Giulio Romano, 1520-24.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE PERSECUTED RELIGION MOVED TOWARD POWER
cards.body: Constantine patronized churches, supported Christian leaders and involved himself in church disputes. Later in the fourth century, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became institutionally privileged as imperial religious policy hardened against traditional cults and rival Christian movements.

cr.artwork: Constantine I Hagia Sophia.jpg
cr.file: Constantine I Hagia Sophia.jpg
cr.line: Constantine I Hagia Sophia.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THIS IS THE HINGE EVERYONE ARGUES ABOUT
cards.body: One ruler's decision moved a persecuted movement to the centre of power. Whether that saved the religion or compromised it is a fight that has run for seventeen centuries.

cr.artwork: Flemish - Constantine the Great at the Milvian Bridge - Walters 371117.jpg
cr.file: Flemish - Constantine the Great at the Milvian Bridge - Walters 371117.jpg
cr.line: Flemish - Constantine the Great at the Milvian Bridge - Walters 371117.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Colossal head of Constantine the Great, c. 312-315 CE, Capitoline Museums, Rome. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Rasputin wouldn't die
stacks.hook: Rasputin was poisoned, shot, beaten, thrown into a freezing river and somehow still wouldn't die. At least, that's the story.

cards.head: Rasputin was poisoned, shot, beaten, thrown into a freezing river and somehow still wouldn't die.
cards.body: At least, that's the story. The legendary death of Russia's most infamous mystic is almost certainly exaggerated. The real murder was dramatic enough without the mythology.

cr.artwork: Grigori Jefimowitsch Rasputin (kop), Bestanddeelnr 917-1738.jpg
cr.file: Grigori Jefimowitsch Rasputin (kop), Bestanddeelnr 917-1738.jpg
cr.line: Grigori Jefimowitsch Rasputin (kop), Bestanddeelnr 917-1738.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: RASPUTIN HAD BECOME CLOSE TO THE ROYAL FAMILY
cards.body: Empress Alexandra believed Rasputin could help her son Alexei, who suffered from hemophilia. His access to the imperial family made him deeply controversial.

cr.artwork: Grigori Rasputin 1916.jpg
cr.file: Grigori Rasputin 1916.jpg
cr.line: Grigori Rasputin 1916.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: A GROUP OF ARISTOCRATS DECIDED TO KILL HIM
cards.body: In December 1916, Prince Felix Yusupov and other conspirators lured Rasputin to the Moika Palace in Petrograd. Yusupov later wrote an extraordinary account of what happened.

cr.artwork: Alexandra Feodorovna, Tsarina of Russia.jpg
cr.file: Alexandra Feodorovna, Tsarina of Russia.jpg
cr.line: Alexandra Feodorovna, Tsarina of Russia.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE CLAIMED POISON DID NOTHING
cards.body: Yusupov said Rasputin consumed cakes and wine laced with cyanide without appearing affected. But later evidence casts serious doubt on whether Rasputin was actually poisoned at all.
cards.cap: Boasson and Eggler St. Petersburg Nevsky 24.

cr.artwork: Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia.jpg
cr.file: Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia.jpg
cr.credit: Boasson and Eggler St. Petersburg Nevsky 24.
cr.line: Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO THEY SHOT HIM
cards.body: The conspirators shot Rasputin multiple times. Yusupov later claimed Rasputin astonishingly got back up and attacked him before being shot again.

cr.artwork: Felix Yusupov Sr..jpg
cr.file: Felix Yusupov Sr..jpg
cr.line: Felix Yusupov Sr..jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN THEY DUMPED HIS BODY
cards.body: Rasputin's body was thrown into the Malaya Nevka River and recovered days later. The famous claim that he survived the shooting and ultimately drowned is not supported by the autopsy evidence generally cited by historians.

cr.artwork: Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin.jpg
cr.file: Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin.jpg
cr.line: Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: RASPUTIN'S OWN KILLERS CREATED THE LEGEND
cards.body: Much of the incredible story comes from Yusupov's later account, and he had every incentive to make the murder sound extraordinary. Rasputin was murdered brutally, but the supposedly supernatural man who refused to die is largely legend.

cr.artwork: Dead Rasputin.jpg
cr.file: Dead Rasputin.jpg
cr.line: Dead Rasputin.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE LEGEND BEAT THE AUTOPSY
cards.body: The 1917 autopsy found no poison and no water in his lungs. The unkillable version comes mainly from Yusupov's memoirs, written in exile after he lost everything, and it is the version everyone repeats.

cr.artwork: After the capture of the Winter Palace. Petrograd. Morning on 26 October 1917.jpg
cr.file: After the capture of the Winter Palace. Petrograd. Morning on 26 October 1917.jpg
cr.line: After the capture of the Winter Palace. Petrograd. Morning on 26 October 1917.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Grigori Rasputin, photographed c. 1916. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Genghis Khan's hidden grave
stacks.hook: Genghis Khan built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Then he made sure nobody could find his grave.

cards.head: Genghis Khan built the largest contiguous land empire in history.
cards.body: Then he made sure nobody could find his grave. Genghis Khan died in 1227, but the location of his burial remains unknown almost 800 years later.

cr.artwork: Genghis Khan（Ming dynasty）.jpg
cr.file: Genghis Khan（Ming dynasty）.jpg
cr.line: Genghis Khan（Ming dynasty）.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HE STARTED AS TEMÜJIN
cards.body: Before becoming Genghis Khan, he was Temüjin, born into the brutal politics of the Mongolian steppe. His father was killed, and his family was abandoned by much of their tribe.

cr.artwork: Mongol Empire at its extent.png
cr.file: Mongol Empire at its extent.png
cr.line: Mongol Empire at its extent.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN HE UNITED THE MONGOLS
cards.body: Through warfare, alliances and political skill, Temüjin defeated rival groups and unified much of the steppe. In 1206, he was proclaimed Genghis Khan.

cr.artwork: Hijra Abyssinia (Rashid ad-Din).jpg
cr.file: Hijra Abyssinia (Rashid ad-Din).jpg
cr.line: Hijra Abyssinia (Rashid ad-Din).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS ARMIES EXPLODED ACROSS ASIA
cards.body: Mongol armies conquered enormous territories across northern China, Central Asia and beyond. Their campaigns were extraordinarily destructive but also created networks connecting distant parts of Eurasia.

cr.artwork: Landscape of Khövsgöl Province.jpg
cr.file: Landscape of Khövsgöl Province.jpg
cr.line: Landscape of Khövsgöl Province.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN GENGHIS KHAN DIED
cards.body: He died in 1227 during a campaign against the Western Xia. Even the precise cause of his death remains uncertain.

cr.artwork: Pursuit by Mongol Warriors (Diez Albums).jpg
cr.file: Pursuit by Mongol Warriors (Diez Albums).jpg
cr.line: Pursuit by Mongol Warriors (Diez Albums).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS BURIAL WAS KEPT SECRET
cards.body: Historical traditions say Genghis Khan wanted an unmarked or concealed burial. Later legends claim everyone who encountered the funeral procession was killed, although these dramatic details are difficult to verify.

cr.artwork: YuanEmperorAlbumGenghisFull.jpg
cr.file: YuanEmperorAlbumGenghisFull.jpg
cr.line: YuanEmperorAlbumGenghisFull.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WE STILL HAVEN'T FOUND HIM
cards.body: Researchers have proposed locations in Mongolia, particularly around the sacred Burkhan Khaldun region, but no tomb has been conclusively identified. One of history's most powerful rulers remains buried somewhere unknown.

cr.artwork: 1784 D'Anville Wall Map of Asia - Geographicus - Asia-anville-1794.jpg
cr.file: 1784 D'Anville Wall Map of Asia - Geographicus - Asia-anville-1794.jpg
cr.line: 1784 D'Anville Wall Map of Asia - Geographicus - Asia-anville-1794.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE GRAVE STAYS HIDDEN
cards.body: He built the largest contiguous land empire in history and then arranged to leave no monument. A man that visible choosing total anonymity is the opposite of what power usually wants.

cr.artwork: YuanEmperorAlbumGenghisPortrait.jpg
cr.file: YuanEmperorAlbumGenghisPortrait.jpg
cr.line: YuanEmperorAlbumGenghisPortrait.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Portrait of Genghis Khan, Yuan dynasty album, 13th-14th century, National Palace Museum, Taipei. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Jesus's lost years
stacks.hook: There is an entire missing period of Jesus's life. The Bible basically jumps from him being 12 to him being around 30.

cards.head: There is an entire missing period of Jesus's life.
cards.body: The Bible basically jumps from him being 12 to him being around 30. They're sometimes called Jesus's "lost years." Despite centuries of speculation, the canonical Gospels tell us almost nothing about them.

cr.artwork: Albrecht-Durer-Christ-with-the-doctors.jpg
cr.file: Albrecht-Durer-Christ-with-the-doctors.jpg
cr.line: Albrecht-Durer-Christ-with-the-doctors.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WE GET STORIES ABOUT HIS BIRTH
cards.body: Matthew and Luke describe events surrounding Jesus's birth and childhood. Luke then tells a story about 12-year-old Jesus discussing Scripture with teachers at the Temple.

cr.artwork: On Nazareth hill (1915) (14761720336).jpg
cr.file: On Nazareth hill (1915) (14761720336).jpg
cr.line: On Nazareth hill (1915) (14761720336).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND THEN...NOTHING
cards.body: After that episode, the narrative jumps forward roughly 18 years. Jesus reappears as an adult around the beginning of his public ministry.

cr.artwork: Jerusalem Modell BW 2.JPG
cr.file: Jerusalem Modell BW 2.JPG
cr.line: Jerusalem Modell BW 2.JPG. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHAT WAS HE DOING?
cards.body: Mark identifies Jesus as a tekton, a Greek term traditionally translated "carpenter" but broad enough to mean a craftsman or builder. The simplest historical possibility is that he spent much of those years living and working in Galilee.

cr.artwork: Eugène Delacroix - Christ on the Sea of Galilee - Walters 37186.jpg
cr.file: Eugène Delacroix - Christ on the Sea of Galilee - Walters 37186.jpg
cr.line: Eugène Delacroix - Christ on the Sea of Galilee - Walters 37186.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: LATER STORIES FILLED IN THE BLANKS
cards.body: Noncanonical writings invented dramatic childhood stories about Jesus performing miracles. In the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, the young Jesus even brings clay birds to life.

cr.artwork: Albrecht Dürer, Christ among the Doctors, c. 1503-1504, NGA 6708.jpg
cr.file: Albrecht Dürer, Christ among the Doctors, c. 1503-1504, NGA 6708.jpg
cr.line: Albrecht Dürer, Christ among the Doctors, c. 1503-1504, NGA 6708.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: MODERN LEGENDS WENT EVEN FURTHER
cards.body: Much later claims have suggested Jesus traveled to India, Tibet or elsewhere during the missing years. Historians have no reliable ancient evidence establishing these journeys.

cr.artwork: Léonard Gaultier, Mary and Joseph Find the Boy Jesus in the Temple with the Doctors, probably c. 1576-1580, NGA 48101.jpg
cr.file: Léonard Gaultier, Mary and Joseph Find the Boy Jesus in the Temple with the Doctors, probably c. 1576-1580, NGA 48101.jpg
cr.line: Léonard Gaultier, Mary and Joseph Find the Boy Jesus in the Temple with the Doctors, probably c. 1576-1580, NGA 48101.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE "LOST YEARS" MAY BE MUCH LESS MYSTERIOUS
cards.body: Ancient biographies didn't necessarily document every stage of someone's life. The Gospel writers were primarily interested in Jesus's ministry, death and resurrection, leaving most of his ordinary early adulthood unrecorded.

cr.artwork: 127790 nazareth-urban landscape PikiWiki Israel.jpg
cr.file: 127790 nazareth-urban landscape PikiWiki Israel.jpg
cr.line: 127790 nazareth-urban landscape PikiWiki Israel.jpg. Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE GAP INVITES INVENTION
cards.body: Eighteen years of silence in the most examined life in history is an opening. Every tradition that wants to claim him has tried to fill it, and none of them can be checked.
cards.cap: James Emery from Douglasville, United States

cr.file: Ancient Grape Processing Plant 0717 (513650020).jpg
cr.credit: James Emery from Douglasville, United States
cr.line: Ancient Grape Processing Plant 0717 (513650020).jpg. Photo: James Emery from Douglasville, United States, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cr.line: Albrecht Durer, Jesus among the Doctors, 1506, Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Where was the Garden of Eden?
stacks.hook: The Garden of Eden supposedly had an address. Genesis actually gives us geographical clues about where it was.

cards.head: The Garden of Eden supposedly had an address.
cards.body: Genesis actually gives us geographical clues about where it was. Genesis describes a river flowing from Eden and dividing into four branches. Two of their names are still extremely familiar: the Tigris and Euphrates.

cr.artwork: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach (I).jpg
cr.file: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach (I).jpg
cr.line: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach (I).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: GENESIS NAMES FOUR RIVERS
cards.body: The rivers are called Pishon, Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates. Genesis also associates them with regions and resources including gold.
cards.cap: Abdul Qadir al-Rassam (1882 - 1952) – painter (Iraqi) Born in Baghdad, Iraq. Died in Bagh

cr.artwork: Abdul Qadir al-Rassam - River Scene on the Banks of the Tigris - Google Art Project.jpg
cr.file: Abdul Qadir al-Rassam - River Scene on the Banks of the Tigris - Google Art Project.jpg
cr.credit: Abdul Qadir al-Rassam (1882 - 1952) – painter (Iraqi) Born in Baghdad, Iraq. Died in Bagh
cr.line: Abdul Qadir al-Rassam - River Scene on the Banks of the Tigris - Google Art Project.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: TWO ARE EASY TO RECOGNIZE
cards.body: The Tigris and Euphrates flow through modern Turkey, Syria and Iraq toward the Persian Gulf. That has naturally led generations of readers to search for Eden somewhere in or near Mesopotamia.

cr.artwork: Cranach der Ältere, Lucas - Paradies, Gal.-Nr. 1908 A.jpg
cr.file: Cranach der Ältere, Lucas - Paradies, Gal.-Nr. 1908 A.jpg
cr.line: Cranach der Ältere, Lucas - Paradies, Gal.-Nr. 1908 A.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE OTHER TWO ARE THE PROBLEM
cards.body: There is no scholarly consensus identifying the Pishon and Gihon with modern rivers. Proposed identifications have ranged across the Middle East and beyond.

cr.artwork: 1865 Spruner Map of Canaan - Mesopotamia crop.jpg
cr.file: 1865 Spruner Map of Canaan - Mesopotamia crop.jpg
cr.line: 1865 Spruner Map of Canaan - Mesopotamia crop.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE GEOGRAPHY DOESN'T MAP NEATLY
cards.body: The four-river description doesn't correspond cleanly to the modern river system. That may be because the geography is ancient, symbolic, literary or based on a worldview very different from a modern map.

cr.artwork: Garden delights.jpg
cr.file: Garden delights.jpg
cr.line: Garden delights.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: PEOPLE HAVE SEARCHED ALL OVER
cards.body: Proposed locations for Eden have included Mesopotamia, Armenia and regions near the Persian Gulf. None has been archaeologically demonstrated to be the biblical garden.

cr.artwork: Adam and Eve - Kunstgewerbemuseum Berlin.jpg
cr.file: Adam and Eve - Kunstgewerbemuseum Berlin.jpg
cr.line: Adam and Eve - Kunstgewerbemuseum Berlin.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EDEN MAY NOT BE A PLACE WE CAN FIND
cards.body: Genesis presents Eden as both a garden and a sacred landscape where humanity lives in God's presence. Whether its geographical clues describe a historical location, symbolic geography or some combination remains debated.

cr.artwork: Map of the Ancient Near East.jpg
cr.file: Map of the Ancient Near East.jpg
cr.line: Map of the Ancient Near East.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY PEOPLE LOOK FOR A LOCATION
cards.body: Two of the four rivers are real and still on maps. That partial match is enough to keep the search alive, because it suggests the rest might be findable too.

cr.artwork: Cranach - Friedländer and Rosenberg, 202.jpg
cr.file: Cranach - Friedländer and Rosenberg, 202.jpg
cr.line: Cranach - Friedländer and Rosenberg, 202.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: Christians who said Jesus didn't suffer
stacks.hook: There were early Christians who believed Jesus didn't actually suffer on the cross.

cards.head: There were early Christians who believed Jesus didn't actually suffer on the cross.
cards.body: Some ancient Christian movements believed Christ was so completely divine that his physical suffering couldn't have happened in the ordinary human sense.

cr.artwork: Matthias Grünewald - The Crucifixion - WGA10723.jpg
cr.file: Matthias Grünewald - The Crucifixion - WGA10723.jpg
cr.line: Matthias Grünewald - The Crucifixion - WGA10723.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE IDEA IS CALLED DOCETISM
cards.body: The name comes from a Greek verb meaning "to seem" or "appear." Broadly, Docetic beliefs held that Jesus's humanity or suffering was only apparent in some sense.

cr.artwork: Cathedral (Monreale) - Left wing transept - West wall - Crucifixion.jpg
cr.file: Cathedral (Monreale) - Left wing transept - West wall - Crucifixion.jpg
cr.line: Cathedral (Monreale) - Left wing transept - West wall - Crucifixion.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE PROBLEM WAS JESUS'S BODY
cards.body: Some early Christians struggled with how a perfect divine being could inhabit corruptible matter, suffer and die. Different groups developed radically different answers.

cr.artwork: Crucifixion of Jesus-Hosios Loukas.jpg
cr.file: Crucifixion of Jesus-Hosios Loukas.jpg
cr.line: Crucifixion of Jesus-Hosios Loukas.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOME SEPARATED JESUS FROM THE DIVINE CHRIST
cards.body: Certain early Christian systems distinguished between the human Jesus and a divine Christ who came upon him. In such systems, the divine element could depart before physical death.

cr.artwork: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg
cr.file: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg
cr.line: Gospel of Thomas - Nag Hammadi II-36.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: OTHER CHRISTIANS HATED THIS IDEA
cards.body: Writers who became foundational to orthodox Christianity insisted that Jesus had genuinely become human. If he didn't really suffer and die, they argued, then the incarnation and resurrection were fundamentally altered.

cr.artwork: CHRIST PANTOCRATOR-SINAI(6th Century).jpg
cr.file: CHRIST PANTOCRATOR-SINAI(6th Century).jpg
cr.line: CHRIST PANTOCRATOR-SINAI(6th Century).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: YOU CAN SEE THE ARGUMENT IN VERY EARLY CHRISTIANITY
cards.body: The letters of John strongly emphasize that Jesus Christ came "in the flesh." Many scholars understand such language against a background of early disputes over Jesus's genuine humanity.

cr.artwork: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Christus am Kreuz - 3242 - Führermuseum.jpg
cr.file: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Christus am Kreuz - 3242 - Führermuseum.jpg
cr.line: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Christus am Kreuz - 3242 - Führermuseum.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: CHRISTIANITY COULD HAVE DEVELOPED VERY DIFFERENTLY
cards.body: The view that Jesus was fully divine and fully human ultimately became central to orthodox Christianity. But the surviving controversies reveal how intensely early Christians disagreed over what it actually meant to call Jesus divine.

cr.artwork: 1290 Mosaikikone mit Kreuzigung Christi Bodemuseum anagoria.JPG
cr.file: 1290 Mosaikikone mit Kreuzigung Christi Bodemuseum anagoria.JPG
cr.line: 1290 Mosaikikone mit Kreuzigung Christi Bodemuseum anagoria.JPG. Photo: Anagoria, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THIS ARGUMENT SHAPED THE CREEDS
cards.body: Whether he actually suffered decides what the death meant. The doctrines were written to close this question, which is why the losing position is still named and rejected by name.

cr.file: The history of the decline and fall of the Roman empire (1909) (14774972781).jpg
cr.line: The history of the decline and fall of the Roman empire (1909) (14774972781).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

stacks.title: 666 and the Roman emperor
stacks.hook: The number 666 wasn't invented as a random spooky number. It may have been a coded reference to an actual Roman emperor.

cards.head: The number 666 wasn't invented as a random spooky number.
cards.body: It may have been a coded reference to an actual Roman emperor. Revelation calls 666 the "number of the beast" and tells readers with wisdom to calculate it. That wording has led scholars to suspect the number encoded a name.

cr.artwork: Civil war and rebellion in the Roman empire A.D. 69-70; companion to the "Histories" of Tacitus (1908) (14576214397).jpg
cr.file: Civil war and rebellion in the Roman empire A.D. 69-70; companion to the "Histories" of Tacitus (1908) (14576214397).jpg
cr.line: Civil war and rebellion in the Roman empire A.D. 69-70; companion to the "Histories" of Tacitus (1908) (14576214397).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: ANCIENT LETTERS COULD ALSO REPRESENT NUMBERS
cards.body: Greek and Hebrew letters had numerical values. Adding the numerical values in a person's name could therefore produce a number, a practice often called gematria.

cr.artwork: 616 name of the beast with ancient greek and roman numerals combined.png
cr.file: 616 name of the beast with ancient greek and roman numerals combined.png
cr.line: 616 name of the beast with ancient greek and roman numerals combined.png. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: NERO FITS REMARKABLY WELL
cards.body: When a form of "Nero Caesar" is written in Hebrew letters, its numerical values can total 666. Nero had become infamous among Christians for his persecution of them in Rome.

cr.artwork: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 3 verso crop Number of the Beast χιϛ 616.jpg
cr.file: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 3 verso crop Number of the Beast χιϛ 616.jpg
cr.line: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 3 verso crop Number of the Beast χιϛ 616.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THERE'S AN EVEN STRANGER CLUE
cards.body: Some ancient manuscripts of Revelation give the number as 616 instead of 666. A different spelling of Nero's name can produce 616, which scholars have cited as evidence supporting the Nero interpretation.

cr.artwork: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 1 verso Rev 2,13–14; 3,10–12; 6,5–6; 9,1–5; 9,7–11.jpg
cr.file: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 1 verso Rev 2,13–14; 3,10–12; 6,5–6; 9,1–5; 9,7–11.jpg
cr.line: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 1 verso Rev 2,13–14; 3,10–12; 6,5–6; 9,1–5; 9,7–11.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: BUT REVELATION'S BEAST IS BIGGER THAN ONE MAN
cards.body: The beast represents political power opposed to God and is closely associated with empire. Even if Nero's name lies behind the number, Revelation's symbolism can operate on multiple levels.

cr.artwork: The number of the beast is 666 Philadelphia, Rosenbach Museum and Library.jpg
cr.file: The number of the beast is 666 Philadelphia, Rosenbach Museum and Library.jpg
cr.line: The number of the beast is 666 Philadelphia, Rosenbach Museum and Library.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: LATER GENERATIONS KEPT FINDING NEW "BEASTS"
cards.body: For centuries, people have manipulated names and numerical systems to make 666 correspond to political leaders, religious figures and enemies. Most such calculations tell us more about the person doing the calculation than Revelation.

cr.artwork: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 2 recto Rev 9,11–16; 9,18–21; 11,1–6; 11,8–12.jpg
cr.file: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 2 recto Rev 9,11–16; 9,18–21; 11,1–6; 11,8–12.jpg
cr.line: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4499 (Papyrus 115) Plate 2 recto Rev 9,11–16; 9,18–21; 11,1–6; 11,8–12.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THE ORIGINAL READERS MAY HAVE UNDERSTOOD THE CODE
cards.body: To a first-century audience living under Roman rule, the imagery may have felt considerably less mysterious than it does today. What became history's most infamous supernatural number may originally have functioned partly as political code.

cr.line: Albrecht Dürer, The Babylonian Whore, probably c. 1496-1498, NGA 6684.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY 666 KEEPS GETTING SOLVED
cards.body: The text invites the reader to calculate it, so every century does. A puzzle with an explicit instruction to solve it will never be left alone.

stacks.title: The Antichrist
stacks.hook: The Antichrist in popular culture is not exactly the Antichrist described in the Bible.

cards.head: The Antichrist in popular culture is not exactly the Antichrist described in the Bible.
cards.body: People imagine one terrifying end-times dictator called "the Antichrist." Surprisingly, the word itself never appears in Revelation.

cr.artwork: Fra angelico luca signorelli orvieto.jpg
cr.file: Fra angelico luca signorelli orvieto.jpg
cr.line: Fra angelico luca signorelli orvieto.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: "ANTICHRIST" APPEARS IN JOHN'S LETTERS
cards.body: The term appears in 1 and 2 John. There, an antichrist is someone who denies fundamental claims about Jesus.

cr.artwork: Gentile da fabriano, madonna di orvieto prima del restauro.jpg
cr.file: Gentile da fabriano, madonna di orvieto prima del restauro.jpg
cr.line: Gentile da fabriano, madonna di orvieto prima del restauro.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND THERE ISN'T JUST ONE
cards.body: First John explicitly says that "many antichrists" have already appeared. That is very different from the single future supervillain of modern popular imagination.

cr.artwork: Ottheinrich Folio295r Rev12.jpg
cr.file: Ottheinrich Folio295r Rev12.jpg
cr.line: Ottheinrich Folio295r Rev12.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: REVELATION HAS A DIFFERENT VILLAIN
cards.body: Revelation describes beasts, including one that exercises enormous authority and receives worship. But Revelation itself doesn't call this figure "the Antichrist."

cr.artwork: B Urgell 209.jpg
cr.file: B Urgell 209.jpg
cr.line: B Urgell 209.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: PAUL HAS ANOTHER MYSTERIOUS FIGURE
cards.body: Second Thessalonians describes a coming "man of lawlessness" who exalts himself and opposes God. Later Christian interpretation connected this figure with the Antichrist.

cr.artwork: Chapel of the Blessed Corporal; Cathedral of Orvieto, Italy..jpg
cr.file: Chapel of the Blessed Corporal; Cathedral of Orvieto, Italy..jpg
cr.line: Chapel of the Blessed Corporal; Cathedral of Orvieto, Italy..jpg. Photo: Georges Jansoone (JoJan), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: EVENTUALLY THE CHARACTERS MERGED
cards.body: Over centuries of Christian interpretation, the antichrist, Revelation's beast and Paul's man of lawlessness became associated with one another. This helped create the familiar idea of one final Antichrist appearing before the end of the world.

cr.artwork: Luca Signorelli - Portrait of an Old Man - Gemäldegalerie Berlin.jpg
cr.file: Luca Signorelli - Portrait of an Old Man - Gemäldegalerie Berlin.jpg
cr.line: Luca Signorelli - Portrait of an Old Man - Gemäldegalerie Berlin.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SO THE POPULAR VERSION IS A COMPOSITE
cards.body: The Bible contains several different evil figures and concepts that later tradition connects. The single charismatic world leader most people picture as "the Antichrist" is a synthesis of multiple biblical passages.

cr.artwork: Duomo Orvieto, Resurrezione della carne, particle.jpg
cr.file: Duomo Orvieto, Resurrezione della carne, particle.jpg
cr.line: Duomo Orvieto, Resurrezione della carne, particle.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE POPULAR VERSION IS BIGGER
cards.body: One terrifying end-times figure is more filmable than a category of people. Cinema needed a villain, and the word does not appear in Revelation at all.

stacks.title: The Ides of March
stacks.hook: Julius Caesar was warned that something terrible would happen on the Ides of March. Then he walked into the Senate anyway.

cards.head: Julius Caesar was warned that something terrible would happen on the Ides of March.
cards.body: Then he walked into the Senate anyway. On March 15, 44 BCE, Caesar was surrounded by senators and stabbed to death. Ancient writers preserve a series of eerie warnings that supposedly preceded the assassination.

cr.artwork: Röm. Republik- M. Iunius Brutus und L. Plaetorius Cestianus - Münzkabinett, Berlin - 5475441.jpg
cr.file: Röm. Republik- M. Iunius Brutus und L. Plaetorius Cestianus - Münzkabinett, Berlin - 5475441.jpg
cr.line: Röm. Republik- M. Iunius Brutus und L. Plaetorius Cestianus - Münzkabinett, Berlin - 5475441.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: A SEER SUPPOSEDLY WARNED HIM
cards.body: Ancient accounts say a soothsayer named Spurinna warned Caesar of danger associated with the Ides of March. The famous phrase "Beware the Ides of March" is Shakespeare's wording, but the underlying warning appears in ancient sources.

cr.artwork: The Death of Caesar by Vincenzo Camuccini, 1804-1805 - Galleria nazionale d'arte moderna - Rome, Italy - DSC05203.jpg
cr.file: The Death of Caesar by Vincenzo Camuccini, 1804-1805 - Galleria nazionale d'arte moderna - Rome, Italy - DSC05203.jpg
cr.line: The Death of Caesar by Vincenzo Camuccini, 1804-1805 - Galleria nazionale d'arte moderna - Rome, Italy - DSC05203.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: HIS WIFE ALSO HAD A NIGHTMARE
cards.body: According to ancient accounts, Caesar's wife Calpurnia had disturbing dreams before the assassination and begged him not to attend the Senate. Caesar initially considered staying home.

cr.artwork: Head of Julius Caesar from Tusculum MAntTorino 2089 n01.jpg
cr.file: Head of Julius Caesar from Tusculum MAntTorino 2089 n01.jpg
cr.line: Head of Julius Caesar from Tusculum MAntTorino 2089 n01.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN ONE OF THE CONSPIRATORS CHANGED HIS MIND
cards.body: Decimus Brutus, a trusted associate who was secretly part of the conspiracy, reportedly persuaded Caesar that staying home because of dreams would look ridiculous. Caesar left for the Senate.

cr.artwork: Capitoline Brutus Musei Capitolini MC1183.jpg
cr.file: Capitoline Brutus Musei Capitolini MC1183.jpg
cr.line: Capitoline Brutus Musei Capitolini MC1183.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: SOMEONE TRIED TO HAND HIM THE ENTIRE PLOT
cards.body: A teacher named Artemidorus reportedly prepared a written warning naming conspirators and tried to give it to Caesar on his way. Caesar never successfully acted on it before entering the meeting.

cr.file: Reconstructie van het Theater van Pompeius te Rome Dimostrazione dell odierno avanzo del teatro di Pompeo (titel op object) Archeologische vondsten in en rond Rome (serietitel) Le Antichità Romane (serietitel), RP-P-OB-36.878.jpg
cr.line: Reconstructie van het Theater van Pompeius te Rome Dimostrazione dell odierno avanzo del teatro di Pompeo (titel op object) Archeologische vondsten in en rond Rome (serietitel) Le Antichità Romane (serietitel), RP-P-OB-36.878.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: THEN THE SENATORS SURROUNDED HIM
cards.body: The conspirators approached Caesar under the pretense of presenting a petition. They suddenly drew their weapons and attacked, stabbing Caesar 23 times.

cr.artwork: Gladiators - wall painting in Pompei, in History of Rome and of the Roman people(1883) (14803382033).jpg
cr.file: Gladiators - wall painting in Pompei, in History of Rome and of the Roman people(1883) (14803382033).jpg
cr.line: Gladiators - wall painting in Pompei, in History of Rome and of the Roman people(1883) (14803382033).jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: AND NO, WE DON'T KNOW THAT HE SAID "ET TU, BRUTE?"
cards.body: Shakespeare immortalized Caesar dying with the words "Et tu, Brute?" Ancient sources give different accounts, including one tradition that Caesar said something in Greek to Brutus, while others say he died silently.

cr.artwork: Assassination of Julius Caesar MET 87.12.171.jpg
cr.file: Assassination of Julius Caesar MET 87.12.171.jpg
cr.line: Assassination of Julius Caesar MET 87.12.171.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: Even the most famous line from Caesar's assassination is probably part of the legend rather than something we can confidently say he spoke.

cr.file: De moord op Julius Ceasar, RP-T-2006-3.jpg
cr.line: De moord op Julius Ceasar, RP-T-2006-3.jpg. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

cards.head: WHY THE IDES BECAME A DATE PEOPLE KNOW
cards.body: Shakespeare gave it a line, and the line gave the date an afterlife. Most Romans died unremembered. This one has a warning attached that people still quote.
